posts.title: An anatomy lesson has a point of view
posts.subtitle: Queer Anatomy Theater borrows the layout of a 1594 dissection room. The record behind it, from Leiden's university archives to a 2022 award jury and a 2026 museum program, shows what a lesson chooses to show and who gets to answer back.
posts.seoTitle: An anatomy lesson has a point of view
posts.description: Queer Anatomy Theater at Dutch Design Week 2026 borrows a 1594 dissection room. What Leiden's archives, award juries and a museum record show.

r: A dissection table in the middle of a ring of seats tells everyone in the room where to look. Kuang-Yi Ku's Queer Anatomy Theater, listed in the Dutch Design Week 2026 program, starts from that arrangement and hands some of the looking back to the participants.

I am an anatomist and medical educator. My studies were in anatomy and neurobiology, and I earned a medical education certificate. That background makes me read an anatomy lesson for its choices: what a model shows, what it leaves out, and who is invited to say so. The program lists the showcase at Plug in City on Strijp-S, Eindhoven, free to enter, daily from 11:00 to 18:00 between October 17 and 25, 2026. It describes four interactive lessons built as a first spatial and participatory test of a larger production still under development.

This essay uses public documents only: the festival listing, the artist's site, award and funder pages, a museum's program, a Leiden doctoral thesis on the original anatomical theater, and two research papers. It reports no visit, no conversation with the artist and no assessment of the medical content. Where a claim is the makers' own, I say so.

blocks.x: A room built to be watched

r: Rijksmuseum Boerhaave in Leiden has the only anatomical theater in the Netherlands, and the museum calls it an exact copy of the theater Leiden University opened in 1594. Its account says the anatomy professor dissected the bodies of hanged criminals there a few times a year, in sessions that ran for several days, and that the audience was made up of students, surgeons and curious citizens who paid to get in.

A 2008 Leiden doctoral thesis by T. Huisman on anatomical practice in seventeenth-century Leiden fills in the room. The university was 18 years old when the theater was put into use at the end of 1594. It was a circular amphitheater with six tiers around a rotatable dissection table, decorated with human and animal skeletons, and it sat in the apse of a secularized church that also held the university library and a fencing school.

Huisman describes the public dissections as conducted with great solemnity, almost like religious ceremonies, attended by the burgomasters of Leiden and the university senate, with other lectures suspended while they took place. One of the banners carried by the skeletons bore the motto "Nosce te ipsum," know thyself.
The museum and the thesis agree on 1594, so I use it. Huisman's own sources are the university's archives, which is the strongest kind of evidence available for a date like this.

What I take from the description is that the arrangement did part of the teaching. Rows of seats, a central table and a person with authority over the body told an audience what a lesson was and who was entitled to explain. Queer Anatomy Theater says it wants to keep the room and change the cast: instead of placing a passive body at the center of medical observation, the program says, participants handle, wear, interpret and remake anatomical knowledge themselves.

blocks.x: The Leiden theater was also a museum, and the two jobs pulled against each other

r: Huisman's thesis adds a complication that earlier histories had skipped. For the rest of the year, when winter dissections were not possible, the theater was open to the public as a collection of rarities. Huisman notes that reports of dissections actually witnessed there are scarce, while many travelers described the skeletons and curiosities on display.
He argues that the two functions, dissection room and cabinet of curiosities, did not coexist comfortably, and that the university archives record conflicts over it through the seventeenth century.

He also shows the room's role shrinking. By his account, Bernard Siegfried Albinus, who became professor in 1719, put more value on anatomical specimens than on public demonstration, and from 1725 he worked in a smaller anatomical theater on the ground floor of another church. After the death of the professor Govert Bidloo in 1712, Huisman writes, the old theater functioned mainly as a museum. It was taken down in 1821 and rebuilt in the Museum Boerhaave toward the end of the twentieth century.

The point for a modern reader is simple. A teaching room's point of view was never fixed. The people who ran it changed what it was for, and the reasons were as much about what counted as good anatomy as about taste. Reworking this room's purpose has a long history, and a queer anatomy theater is the latest entry in it.

blocks.x: A project that began as a book

r: Queer Anatomy Theater is the second phase of a project that started on paper. The first phase, the Atlas of Queer Anatomy, was made by Ku with Henry de Vries, a professor and physician who works on sexually transmitted infections. The Boerhaave program describes De Vries as a dermatologist and professor of skin infections at the University of Amsterdam, working at the Academic Medical Center and the Public Health Service of Amsterdam. It describes Ku as a former dentist, bio-artist and speculative designer who lives between Taiwan and the Netherlands and is doing a PhD at Sheffield Hallam University.
The DDW listing credits De Vries as the showcase's medical and scientific collaborator.

The sequence of events is documented in several places. In June 2022 the Bio Art & Design Award chose the project, then titled Filthy Anatomy, as one of three winning teams from a long list of 120 proposals, with 25,000 euros each to develop an installation.
The award's own page describes it as a challenge to the medical patriarchy and heteronormativity of anatomical education, built from what it calls speculative queer anatomies.
MU Hybrid Art House in Eindhoven showed it in Beyond Borders & Binaries from December 16, 2022 to April 16, 2023, with the other two winning teams and five other projects.

Ku's own page, which reproduces MU's text, describes the first two chapters and credits the book design and video to Tzu-yen Chen of Onieyen Studio, the same studio credited for visual design at DDW 2026.
The Core77 entry says Chapter 1 is on the transmission of sexually transmitted infections and Chapter 2 on intersex.
Recognition followed. Core77 listed it as a winner of its 2023 Speculative Design Award, which the Boerhaave program specifies as the professional winner.
The Dutch Design Awards listed it as a 2023 nominee in Design Research.
The Creative Industries Fund NL says it granted the atlas 30,000 euros in 2023.
The Prix Ars Electronica archive lists an honorary mention in 2025 in the Artificial Life & Intelligence category.
The book, 176 pages, came out in 2025 from Limestone Books.
I corrected one item while reading. A university news page about the project says it won the Dutch Design Awards in Design Research.
The awards' own gallery page labels the project a nominee, and the same page's related list marks a different project as the 2023 Design Research winner.

blocks.x: Where the Netter date does not hold

r: Most descriptions of the atlas define it against a famous book. The Bio Art & Design Award page, the Core77 entry, the Dutch Design Awards gallery and the funder's article all place it as a reflection on Frank H. Netter's Atlas of Human Anatomy and give 1957 as the year that book first appeared.

I could not confirm that date. The Open Library catalog, which gathers library records, lists the earliest edition of "Atlas of human anatomy" as published by Ciba-Geigy in 1989, with the Library of Congress control number 89060477.
Netter's earlier Ciba Collection of Medical Illustrations began in 1953, and its volume on the liver, biliary tract and pancreas is dated 1957 in the Garrison-Morton listing.
My guess, and it is only a guess, is that the 1957 comes from a volume of that older series and was carried into the project descriptions. No source I found says so.

The critique does not depend on the date. Whether a reference atlas dates from 1957 or 1989, the question about whose body it treats as the reference remains. But a lesson about checking what a standard source says is a good place to be careful about the date, and I would rather say what I found than repeat it.

blocks.x: Four lessons, four kinds of claim

r: The program lists the four lessons in one paragraph, and I find it useful to ask of each what kind of claim it makes.

Lesson One is a CAPTCHA-style game comparing homologous structures in embryonic sex development, which the program says questions binary teaching models. That bundles a biological statement with a statement about teaching. The biology is that some adult structures share an embryonic origin. A cell-lineage study in mice, published in Scientific Reports, calls the genital tubercle the precursor of the penis and clitoris and notes that early development of the external genitalia is conserved across most amniote vertebrates.

The teaching statement is about how textbooks present sex. Of that, a systematic analysis of 6,044 images from 17 anatomy textbooks used at Australian medical schools, published between 2008 and 2013, found that images remain predominantly male outside sex-specific sections and that the books adhere almost completely to a sex and gender binary.
Lesson Two turns gender-affirming surgery into a collaborative garment-based exercise.
The Boerhaave program for the atlas asks why gender-affirming surgeries are so absent from anatomy textbooks, which suggests the lesson carries a chapter's question into a room.

Here the claim is a proposal about representation and participation. It does not claim to teach a surgical technique, and the program says nothing that would let a reader treat it as clinical instruction.
Lesson Three uses a photo booth to map encounters between flesh and sex toys and produces what the program calls a Pleasure Counterfoil.
Lesson Four combines clay modeling and augmented-reality filters to make short videos about sexuality, microorganisms and interspecies relations.

The Boerhaave page lists the atlas's themes as sexually transmitted infections as an interplay between bodies and microorganisms, intersex anatomy, gender-affirming surgery, body odors and sex toys. The lessons echo those themes, though no source I found says which lesson derives from which chapter.

blocks.x: What the research on teaching adds, and where it stops

r: Two papers help frame the stakes. A 2011 survey of deans at 176 medical schools in Canada and the United States found a median of five hours spent on LGBT-related content in the whole curriculum, with 33.3 percent of responding schools reporting zero hours during the clinical years.
The textbook analysis above found a male-dominated, binary visual record.

Both have limits that matter here. The survey covers North America in 2009 and 2010 and reports hours and deans' own ratings more than what students learned. The textbook study covers Australian books and does not single out Netter. Neither tells us how Dutch medical schools teach this material today, and neither tests whether a participatory exercise changes what a learner understands. I found no evaluation of that kind for the atlas workshops or for the theater. The one outcome claim I found comes from the makers: the fund's article says some doctors who took part in workshops brought the methods into their own teaching.
That is Ku's report in a feature article that quotes him, and I have no independent confirmation.

blocks.x: Who can question the lesson?

r: My main interest is a documented moment in the earlier workshops. According to the Creative Industries Fund NL article, medical professionals responded positively to the themes of diversity and inclusion but also raised concrete criticism. Some participants pointed out that the atlas images still follow the conventional approach of showing the body as separate organs. The reported response was to encourage participants to disrupt the images, deconstructing and reassembling them.
Ku is quoted saying that kind of feedback takes the project beyond the makers' own perspectives.

I read that as a good sign for the form and an incomplete one for the evidence. A lesson that invites a challenge and changes in response has a point of view that can move, like the Leiden room did. But the account comes from the maker, and I cannot see how many participants raised the objection or what changed afterward. The program page for DDW 2026 does not describe how a visitor can disagree with a lesson, or what happens to a correction.

It also helps that the atlas has been shown in places with different expectations. The fund's article says that in art settings it is read as critical or speculative, while in medical settings the reactions were described as more direct and practical, and it names Amsterdam UMC and the Taipei Fine Arts Museum among the venues.

In March 2025 the project was invited into Unseen, an exhibition at Rijksmuseum Boerhaave that ran from March 7, 2025 to March 8, 2026 on how medicine has overlooked women and gender-diverse people. The museum's page names the atlas as one of the contemporary perspectives in the show.
The museum that holds the 1594-style theater showed the atlas, though none of the sources I found says whether the two were displayed near each other.

The curator, Mieneke te Hennepe, said in an interview published in Nursing Clio on July 23, 2025 that the idea for Unseen came partly from her lecture on the history of women in medicine at Leiden University Medical Center, and partly from the museum wanting to see its medical collections through a different lens.
That is a different kind of institution acting on a similar question: who is missing from the standard picture.

blocks.x: The audience is another relationship

r: The DDW page describes a future form in which medical students and healthcare professionals become the primary participants in a fictional anatomy school, revisiting subjects they once met in conventional education. Interviews would ask them to reflect on the earlier classroom and the new lessons. The general public would be a second layer of spectatorship, following the encounters through a reality-show-style social media broadcast.

The funder's article says the format deliberately borrows from popular culture and that social media gives broader access to medical knowledge than a textbook, and that a 50,000 euro grant was recently awarded to the follow-up project. That article is undated, so I cannot place the grant.

The Leiden record shows that a paying public was part of the room from its first years. Huisman calls the theater a seventeenth-century tourist attraction of the first order, and the museum says curious citizens paid an entrance fee.

A broadcast is a different way to sell and spend attention, and the sources describe the future format only in outline. They do not say who will record what, what participants will agree to, who edits a clip, or whether a person can take part in a lesson without being filmed. Those are the questions I would want answered before judging the format, and the program page is not the place that answers them.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: No photograph or report of the 2026 lessons exists yet. The program page carries renders and interface images, and the showcase opens October 17, 2026.
I found no evaluation of whether the atlas workshops or the theater improve anyone's understanding, and no study of how Dutch medical schools teach these topics.
The 1957 date for Netter's atlas conflicts with catalog records that give 1989. The source of the 1957 is unclear.
The date and size of the grant for the theater come from one undated page.
It is not stated whether the atlas was in Unseen from its opening on March 7, 2025, or joined in March. The launch page says it was invited in March 2025.
Which lessons derive from which atlas chapters is not stated in the sources I found.
Consent, recording and broadcast terms for the future reality-show format are not described.
The exact date the Leiden theater was rebuilt at Boerhaave is given only as the end of the twentieth century.

r: If you go, a useful way to take a lesson is to ask three things at the table. Who chose this example? What would a different example have shown? And how would I know if the model were wrong?

posts.title: When does a find become a feedstock?
posts.subtitle: Dutch law says every archaeological find from an excavation must be kept. EX SITU, at Dutch Design Week 2026, works with finds that were deselected. The government inspectorate's own 2025 report shows how that decision gets made, and what is still unsettled.
posts.seoTitle: When does a find become a feedstock?
posts.description: EX SITU at Dutch Design Week 2026 uses deselected archaeological finds. What the Heritage Act and the 2025 inspectorate report say about that decision.

r: Under the Dutch Heritage Act, an archaeological find that comes out of an excavation is meant to be kept. The state inspectorate that supervises the system wrote in 2025 that, in practice, some finds have always been left behind or thrown away, and that nobody has settled how that should be governed.

EX SITU – Matter in Translation, in the Dutch Design Week 2026 program, begins from that gap. It presents nine designer-artists making new work from archaeological finds that were deselected, a word the program uses for objects and fragments not selected for museum collections.

I read this as a question about records. When a find becomes a material, who made the decision, at which stage, and what stays attached to the object afterward? This essay uses public documents only: the program pages for the project and its nine participants, the Heritage Act, the inspectorate's report and the ministry papers around it, the provincial depot's pages, a European archiving standard and two pieces of research on Roman timber. It reports no visit, no interview and no inspection of any object. Where a statement is the project's own, I say so.

blocks.x: The law says keep everything

r: The Heritage Act (Erfgoedwet), in the consolidated version valid from January 1, 2026, defines an archaeological find as a remnant, object or other trace of human presence in the past that comes from an archaeological monument.

A find from an excavation that nobody can prove they own belongs to the province where it was found, or to a municipality that has a designated depot, or to the state if it was found outside any municipality.
The province must keep a depot where finds can be stored in a way that is responsible in terms of conservation and accessibility.
A firm that excavates under the system's certificate must conserve what it finds and hand it, with the documentation, to the owner within two years.

The inspectorate reads these provisions, and the explanatory memoranda behind them, as requiring that every find from an excavation be kept, with no distinction by type, material, size, condition or rarity. Its own illustration is blunt: every scrap of charcoal and every roof tile should in principle be kept, whether there are two shards or two thousand.

The Act also lets the minister, within six months of the notification of first findings, decide that a find owned by a province or municipality is placed under the management of a museum institution because of its public interest.
None of this mentions design. It tells us who owns a find and where it is supposed to go.

blocks.x: Practice has always selected, and the rules say so only indirectly

r: In 2025 the Inspectorate for Government Information and Heritage (Inspectie Overheidsinformatie en Erfgoed) published "Van vondst tot vuilnis," Dutch for "From find to rubbish," an exploratory study of what the system calls deselection: finds that are left in the field, not handed to a depot, or later removed from one.
Its summary states the contradiction directly. The Act leaves no room for leaving finds on an excavation site or removing them from a depot, and it has happened for as long as anyone can remember.
The inspectorate sent the report to the ministry on November 11, 2025.
The picture it draws is of limited, restrained practice, resting on self-reported survey answers that it says it could not validate.

In the 2023 to 2024 monitor, 60 to 65 percent of certificate holders said they take all finds from the field. Most prepare a list of finds to remove before handing material to a depot (84 percent), though they say they do it for only some projects and to a limited extent. About 70 percent of depots say they never refuse finds at the gate. About half remove finds from the depot at some point, with great restraint and in very small numbers.
The reasons given are mostly practical: recent date, unclear context, danger such as mold, finds that have crumbled to dust, or bulk urban material such as stone walls and wooden wells.

The report says most certificate holders and depots have no written policy on deselection. It does not read that as an absence of rules. Retention is treated as the rule and deselection as the exception, and the sector's own quality standard, the Kwaliteitsnorm Nederlandse Archeologie (KNA), has carried procedures for it for more than 15 years.
Under that standard a proposal to remove finds is made with a material specialist, and the rules require that the selection always be submitted to the depot for approval.

The inspectorate's concern is documentation. Deselected finds are often not fully described or identified, and sampling before removal is the exception. It points out that such decisions then cannot be checked, especially when one person makes them.
Its conclusion was that neither stricter enforcement nor a change in the law was needed, and it warned that writing an exception into the Act could encourage less restraint.

The sector did not simply agree. A January 5, 2026 note to the minister, prepared by the heritage directorate, records that several parties in the field, including the national heritage agency and municipal and provincial depot holders, did not recognize themselves in the inspectorate's conclusions.

In a letter to parliament on February 2, 2026, the minister of education, culture and science, G. Moes, sent the report and said other signals had also reached him. He will weigh the report within the process of revising the Heritage Act and decide whether a change on this point remains desirable.
As of that letter, the question was open.

That history is old. The report quotes fragments of notes, minutes and articles from 1990 to 1994 held in the national archive. One says excavation is the ultimate selection. Another asks whether this generation has the right to dispose of anything. A third calls the unanswered question who gets the authority, and the knowledge, to deselect.

The report adds that depots still hold large amounts of material that has never been worked up. It cites an estimate of about 8,000 excavations in the twentieth century, of which about 4,000 were never worked up, and says a well-founded selection is hard to make while a depot lacks a full picture of its collection.

blocks.x: Where deselected finds go

r: The default fate in the sector is destruction. Under the quality standard, finds that do not go to a depot are in principle offered for destruction so that they cannot end up back in the soil archive by mistake. Thirty-seven percent of certificate holders say they destroy all deselected finds, through the ordinary trash or a scrap dealer. Five percent say they keep everything themselves, use it for teaching or give it to amateur societies or local museums. The rest destroy some and send some elsewhere. The report lists amateur societies (34 percent), local museums (22 percent), schools and educational use (22 percent), reference collections and ArcheoHotspots (10 percent) and, at the end of the list, an end use as an art object (2 percent).
The passage does not say what the percentages are a share of, so I treat them as rough.

Depots mostly destroy removed finds too, for a stated reason: so that there is no chance the object resurfaces somewhere as a find without context. Five depots give removed finds to amateur societies, local museums or an educational institution.

I find that destruction rationale the most useful sentence in the report for thinking about design. The profession's worry about a deselected object is that it will turn up later with no record of where it came from. A well-documented design use is the opposite situation, but only if the documentation exists.

blocks.x: The vocabulary is doing work

r: The project's materials use three phrases that are not interchangeable. The program calls the material deselected and describes it as not selected for museum collections.
Lotte Douwes's page calls her ceramic finds deaccessioned.
Judith Sanders's page calls the oak and leather deselected for museum collections or further research.
In the inspectorate's report, deselection is a decision taken at one of three moments: in the field, during working-up before transfer to a depot, or by a depot.
Deaccessioning is what a museum does when it removes an object from a collection. A museum collection is not the same thing as a provincial depot, which holds finds because the Act says it must.

So "deselected from what?" has at least three answers, and the program page does not say which applies to which object. It says the material was made available by the Provincial Archaeological Depot, Archaeology The Hague, Archaeology Rotterdam, Heritage Delft, Heritage Leiden, ADC Archaeology, Archol, IDDS and RAAP.

The inspectorate's appendices list ADC, Archol, IDDS and RAAP among the excavating firms not tied to government, and the Provincial Depot Zuid-Holland among the depots, along with municipal archaeology bodies in The Hague, Delft and Rotterdam.
So the list mixes depot keepers with firms that excavate, and under the Act the owner of a find can be a province or a municipality.
I cannot tell from the pages which organization decided on which object, or under which of the sector's procedures.
The title has its own history. In the inspectorate's account, the system exists to keep finds "ex situ," outside the ground, in a depot.
I found no statement from the project about why it chose the term, and I draw no conclusion from it.

blocks.x: What the nine participants say they are doing

r: EX SITU is an initiative of the curator and designer Marisa Klaster and the archaeological advisor René Isarin. The program says their first joint project was Vases of Roman Limes Wood in 2022.
A Homo Faber listing describes those vases as hand-turned from oak foundation poles used in building Roman Limes roads around 125 AD, preserved with a bio-resin and then turned on a lathe.

The program names the Province of South Holland as a partner and Boskalis Nederland as principal sponsor, and says Boskalis cares about the careful management of archaeological heritage and about reuse of archaeological materials. That is the company's stated position.

The program lists the materials as ceramics, glass, leather, wood, metal, natural stone, mammoth bone and flint. At DDW 2026, it says, EX SITU is a first viewing of experiments and objects the designers are working on. A public exhibition at See Lab The Hague from February 5 to March 7, 2027 will show their final objects next to a curated selection of South Holland heritage artifacts made available by the provincial depot.
The individual pages say more about what is done to the material, and it ranges widely.
Some pages describe shaping and setting. Judith Bloedjes sets archaeological clay pipes and flint in jewelry.
Daan Simons, whose page describes his practice as glue-free wood joinery, builds footed pots from archaeological wood, 14th century and later, meant to hold a memory or the ashes of a loved one.
Willem van Hooff combines 14th and 15th century wood and stone.

Judith Sanders makes a high-heeled shoe from oak from the Roman Limes road of 125 AD and a sneaker from medieval leather, and says the material is placed in current footwear construction without disguising its age or origin.

Other pages describe changes of state. Lotte Douwes says the first melting tests and samples of Roman sigillata shards will be on view, to be developed into objects that refer back to the material's history.
Natasja van der Meer turns eight materials, some about 20,000 years old, into glazes for porcelain plates.
Matthias Quadekker forges a sword from Roman nails, an 18th-century cannonball and Rotterdam wood from about 1300.
Shahar Livne carves and engraves 50,000-year-old mammoth bone for a work questioning the ethics of de-extinction.

Melting, glazing and forging cannot be reversed. Shaping a heel from oak or setting flint in a ring changes an object less, though I cannot tell from the pages how much. The inspectorate's recommendation contains a sentence that applies here: finds can only be removed and destroyed once, and afterward they are gone for good.

It does not follow that melting a shard is wrong. It follows that the decision to melt it is the kind of decision the inspectorate wants documented, and the program pages do not say how it was documented.

blocks.x: A record that follows the object

r: The inspectorate recommends that any find removed be extensively documented, identified and, where suitable, sampled, so that its potential for future research is kept as far as possible.

The European standard for archaeological archives, EAC Guidelines 1, has several requirements that read as if written for this situation. Every archive item should carry a unique identifier. Selection criteria and procedures must be fully documented and included in the archive. Finds that are discarded should be documented as discarded, with when and why, and the location of any reburied find recorded.

The standard is about archives, not about design, and it does not address reuse. It gives a vocabulary for what a before-and-after photograph would need behind it. Anatomy collections run on a similar principle, since a specimen serves teaching only while its record stays attached, and I offer that as a comparison and not as a rule for archaeology.

There is a concrete reason the record matters for the Roman oak. The abstract of Ronald Visser's doctoral thesis at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam reports that wood used to build a road along the limes in the Netherlands was felled in a single season in AD 124 to 125, came from a woodland between the Rhine and the Meuse, and was carried more than 100 kilometers.

The tree-ring dating behind that finding was published in 2015 in the Journal of Archaeological Science under the title "Imperial timber? Dendrochronological evidence for large-scale road building along the Roman limes in the Netherlands."
That information lives in the rings of the wood itself.

I do not know that the oak in Sanders's shoe or Klaster's earlier vases comes from the excavations in that study. The pages say 125 AD and the Roman Limes road. They do not name a site. The point is narrower. Wood from such a road can carry dated and sourced information, and shaping it into a heel decides what remains readable. It also raises a practical question that the program does not answer: whether the finds were sampled and documented before they were deselected, and who holds those records.

Credit can follow the same specificity. The artists' names are on the pages. The program names nine organizations as providers. It does not tie any provider to any piece, and it names no earlier maker, which is honest, since most are unknown.

blocks.x: A loan is a different route

r: The provincial depot describes itself as accepting finds and documentation from professionals and as lending finds to museums and researchers. Its page invites museums, universities and other cultural institutions to borrow finds, with a request at least four weeks ahead.

The depot's three-page loan procedure adds that a loan contract is made only with staff of an institution, never with an individual. The borrower insures the objects, the depot manager can inspect or end the loan, and the objects must go back to the depot.
I found no clause in those pages about altering an object.
That matters because the exhibition in The Hague will show finds from the depot next to the new work.

A loan keeps the object as it is and sends it home. A deselection gives up the decision to keep it. The program does not say whether the finds in 2027 are loans. And seeing an object, borrowing it, photographing it and transforming it are different acts, each of which would need its own permission.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: Which deselection stage each object went through (field, working-up, depot), who approved it and under which KNA procedure.
Which provider supplied which object, and who owned it under the Act (a province, a municipality or a certificate holder awaiting transfer).
Whether finds were documented, identified or sampled before they were changed, and who holds those records.
Whether any provider's material is on loan, or has been given outright.

Whether the mammoth bone is an archaeological find under the Act, which requires a trace of human presence, or came from an excavation at all. The program lists it among the project's archaeological finds.
How the oak relates to the sites in the dated Limes road studies.
What Heesen's glass project will show. His page was not among those I could read, and I make no statement about it.
How the inspectorate's percentages for reuse destinations were calculated, and how the minister will decide after the Heritage Act review.

r: The question in the title has an answer I can offer only in outline. A find becomes a feedstock when someone with the authority decides it will not be kept as a find, and the responsible version of that decision leaves a record. If you stand in front of an object at EX SITU, you could ask for three things: which find it was, who decided, and where its record is kept.

posts.title: Do we want the biology alive, or the material to last?
posts.subtitle: Two Dutch Design Week 2026 projects start from living matter and want opposite things from it. One arrests decay, the other depends on growth. The makers' own records and the research on fungi and preserved specimens show what each asks of an object, and what the listings leave out.
posts.seoTitle: Alive, or built to last? Two DDW wearables
posts.description: Bio Art Fashion arrests decay; KojiGotchi depends on growth. What the makers' records and the research on fungi and herbaria show.

r: Two wearables in the Dutch Design Week 2026 program start from living matter and want opposite things from it. Agnes van Dijk's Bio Art Fashion takes seaweed, fungi, lichen and plant residue and makes them stop changing. KojiGotchi, by Maxim Velli and Rasmus Tofthøj, gives a fungus a body-warm home and asks its wearer to keep it growing.

As an anatomist I am used to the difference between living tissue and preserved tissue: they are different kinds of evidence and they answer different questions. That habit is why I want to compare these two. The word "biological" describes where a material came from. It does not say whether the material is growing, dormant or fixed, and each state asks something different of the object and its owner. This essay uses public documents only: the festival's program pages, the makers' own sites and experiment records, a genome study of the koji fungus, a research abstract on inactivating fungal materials and a botanical garden's account of its herbarium. It reports no visit, no test of any sample and no interview. Where a statement is the maker's, I say so.

blocks.x: What each project says it is

r: Bio Art Fashion is a series of sculptural wearable artworks made from seaweed, mushrooms, lichen and other organic residual materials, shown at VEEM floor 8 on Strijp-S, the home of Manifestations. The program says Van Dijk uses a self-developed, non-toxic preservation technique, and that the materials remain flexible, skin-friendly and repairable while their organic character stays visible.

Van Dijk's own site describes her as preserving ephemeral organic substances by "mummifying" them, making what it calls lace from cabbage leaves and leather from mandarin peel, and says the fabrics are skin-friendly, moisture resistant and easy to repair.
It lists five pieces as on display at DDW 2026: Luffa, a cactus skeleton dress, WeedWave, Mysterious Connections (material: fungi) and Mosss (material: moss and latex).

The program for her 2025 showing, MandarinSkin, Roots & Flowers, used almost the same words. It described a technique refined over a few years and said the material can withstand stress, is skin-friendly, moisture resistant and easy to restore.
So the claims have been in the public program for at least two Octobers. Neither listing cites a test, a duration or a method.

KojiGotchi is described in the program as an open-source wearable that uses human body heat to grow Aspergillus oryzae, the fungus behind miso and sake, in a transparent chamber, with a digital avatar called KojiMoji that reads live sensor data and turns conditions into emotional states. It is listed at BioArt Laboratories, Strijp T+R.
The team developed it at DTU Biosustain in Copenhagen for the 2025 Biodesign Challenge, where it was a finalist, with supervision by Joshua Evans and Adrien Rigobello.
The listing says the device is designed for primary schools, maker spaces and home kitchens, and that visitors can observe the chamber directly.

blocks.x: "Biological" covers at least three states

r: A fungus can be growing, dormant or dead, and a plant can be fresh, dried or fixed in fluid. A photograph of any of them can look biological. The difference is a matter of evidence.

Mycelium-based materials make the point. A 2023 conference abstract from researchers at the Universidade Católica Portuguesa describes how such biocomposites are made: sterilize the biomass, inoculate it with fungi, incubate it, then interrupt or inactivate the fungal growth. Most go through a heat treatment, which the authors say leaves the material rigid and low in flexibility.

They tested gentler options, low-temperature treatments and a copper sulfate spray, on composites from two fungal strains, with a cell viability assay as the measure. Two days after a low-temperature treatment viability looked like about 1 percent. Fifteen days later it was about 34 percent, and the authors concluded the fungus had been left dormant, not killed.

It is a one-page abstract and it studies different fungi from the ones in these exhibits. What it shows is that a material can test as inactive and then resume growth, and that flexibility and certainty of inactivation pull in different directions.

Preserved plant collections show the opposite end. The Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh describes a herbarium of more than three million preserved specimens that spans more than 300 years. Its oldest specimens date to the 1600s, and its specimens are dried or kept in preserving fluid before being cataloged and stored in cabinets.
The garden says DNA can be extracted from specimens in the collection.
A herbarium sheet is dead and still evidence. The garden says the collection needs ongoing care and conservation, and its care pages include integrated pest management.
A wearable is handled, folded and put on a body, and nothing in either listing suggests that the herbarium's methods apply to it.
None of this tells us what is in the exhibits. It gives a vocabulary for asking.

blocks.x: Preservation is a claim about time

r: For Bio Art Fashion the question is how long the form stays as it is and what is meant by "repairable." A repair implies that something changes and someone intervenes. The listing does not say what change is expected, over how long, or what a repair involves.
A herbarium works with a similar logic: the specimen is stable because the conditions around it are managed.
A garment that is worn is not in a cabinet.
The artist's site also shows how the pieces are described. It says she "immortalizes" ephemeral materials and celebrates the beauty of decay.
That is a statement of intent, and it sits beside a different phrase, that the preserving mixture provides "reliable extension."

An honest account of such a piece would give the date a material was collected, the date it was treated and the date its condition was last recorded. The site dates some pieces to earlier Dutch Design Weeks, and it is not always clear which. One heading reads "Alive | DDW2024" above text that says the project would be revealed at the 2023 edition.
I cannot tell from the pages which of the 2026 works are older.

The "skin-friendly" claim deserves a sentence on its own, because it is the claim a reader might act on. Neither listing cites a test. The site lists latex as a material in two pieces, Mosss and an orchid ensemble, without saying what kind.
The U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health says latex exposure can cause allergic reactions in some workers and notes that such reactions have increased among health care workers.

I am not suggesting the pieces cause harm. I am saying that "skin-friendly" is a statement about specific ingredients and specific people, and the pages do not say how it was judged. This essay gives no health advice and takes no position on the pieces.

blocks.x: Growth is a claim about conditions

r: KojiGotchi's maker records are unusually open, and they show what growth takes. In the team's experiment log, the first attempt put steamed rice and koji spores in a zip-lock bag in a back pocket for 48 hours and produced minimal to no visible growth. The team writes that it could not tell whether temperature, humidity or contamination was to blame.

A second run kept a 3D-printed egg-shaped container, with a sensor and no koji inside, under an armpit and logged temperatures within the 25 to 35 degree Celsius range the team gives as koji's ideal. In a final proof of concept with a transparent chamber, the log reports growth over 60 hours that took slightly longer than in a traditional incubator, with the resulting koji just as fragrant and tasty.
The log also says that overheating inside the rice clump made the koji prone to contamination, and that mold color is a key visual cue for it.
The log adds that the first two of four tries in its sensor experiment failed for various reasons.
Those are the makers' reports, with small numbers: the sensor graphs note n of 2 and 3.

They are useful because they name what can go wrong. The device's avatar reads temperature, humidity, volatile organic compounds and carbon dioxide, and the makers say the smell of koji gives immediate sensory feedback on whether care is working.

The team chose koji on purpose. Their product-design page says they first looked at bacterial cellulose from kombucha and at mycelium, and found that those materials thrive at room temperature and resist contamination, demanding little effort. Koji, which needs warmth and attention, fit the dynamic engagement they wanted.
Their portfolio page says that neglect or attention directly determines both the device's functionality and the organism's fate.
So the design intends an organism that can fail, and a wearer who is partly responsible for whether it does.

The biology behind the species matters for how to read "the fungus behind miso and sake." A 2012 genome study in Current Biology describes Aspergillus oryzae as a domesticated fungus whose saccharification abilities humans have used for thousands of years, and its wild relative Aspergillus flavus as a potentially toxigenic plant and animal pathogen. The two species share 99.5 percent of their genome sequence.

The authors describe A. oryzae as an atoxigenic domesticate recognized by the U.S. Department of Agriculture as generally regarded as safe, and A. flavus as a producer of the carcinogen aflatoxin. Their data suggest that an atoxigenic lineage of A. flavus evolved into the "cell factory" used for sake.
They also note that in sake making the fungus grows on steamed rice for about two days before the rice is fermented with yeast.

That last detail shows a difference in time. Traditionally, koji growth is a stage with an end. KojiGotchi turns it into a relationship with a duration, and its pages do not say how long a chamber is meant to run, what a wearer does when the growth ends, or what happens to the organism after.

The species facts also show where the sources stop. The genome study is about domesticated lineages in general. It does not tell us the identity of the strain in a given device, or how likely contamination is in a home kitchen. The makers say rice and koji spores are easily ordered online, and that the device is designed for schools and home kitchens.

The pages I read do not describe a contamination protocol or safety guidance for wearers. I raise that as a question. I give no safety advice, and a person who wants it should ask the makers or a qualified microbiologist.

blocks.x: What the makers' own user study found

r: The KojiGotchi team ran a two-part study, an interactive session and an online survey, and published the findings. In the interactive session, participants smelled, touched and optionally tasted koji, then set up the device themselves with grains of their choice and rice flour standing in for spores.

The team reports that participants were excited about futuristic biodesign but mostly wary of contamination and allergy concerns with living materials. Many became reluctant to touch the koji rice again once they learned it was essentially moldy rice. They preferred white koji, and found black and green varieties too dangerous in appearance.
The page says not a single participant considered or attempted to work in a sterile manner while setting up the device.

The online survey reports that 84.78 percent of respondents were curious about or comfortable with giving body heat, breath or sweat to power microbial growth, and that 39.13 percent would trust food fermented by such a device. Respondents' leading concerns were infection or contamination and hygiene.
Those percentages are consistent with 46 respondents, which is my arithmetic: the page I read does not state how many people answered, or how they were recruited.

This is a maker's study, not a peer-reviewed one. I include it because it is the clearest statement in the sources of the gap the project says it wants to close, and because the one behavior it records, no one working sterile, is the point where a growth-oriented object depends on a person. The team's stated reason for the Tamagotchi format is to teach care while avoiding extreme direct exposure to microbes.
A preserved garment asks something else of its wearer, which is not to damage it.

blocks.x: Three designs, three kinds of time

r: Put together, the sources outline three ways a living material can enter a designed object.

The first is to stop it early and keep the form, which is Bio Art Fashion's stated aim. The success condition is stability, and the evidence would be a treatment record, dates and a record of condition.

The second is to grow it and then stop it, which is how most mycelium composites are made. The success condition is a finished material that stays inactive, and the evidence would be a viability measure taken more than once, since the dormancy result shows one reading can mislead.

The third is to keep it growing and make the wearer responsible, which is KojiGotchi's stated aim. The success condition is continued growth under care, and the evidence would be a log of conditions, strain identity and dates.

What each design counts as failure differs too. For the preserved work it could be a visible change. For the growing device it is neglect, overheating or contamination, and the team's own log shows those outcomes are real.
The two listings tell me what the makers hope for and say little about what failure would look like.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: Which preservation method Van Dijk uses, how long a treated sample has been observed, and what "repairable" involves.
Whether the "skin-friendly" claim was tested, and what the latex in two pieces is.
Which of the five 2026 works are new and which were shown earlier.
Whether the KojiGotchi chamber at the exhibition holds a growing culture, and for how long it can run.
The strain, the contamination rate and any safety protocol for wearers, beyond the team's note that no study participant worked sterile.
How many people took part in the interactive session and the survey, and how they were recruited.
What happens to the organism, and to the device, when growth ends.
Whether the makers intend to produce the device, which the project site invites visitors to signal an interest in, and on what terms.
How the Kew herbarium, which an earlier draft of this essay cited, compares. Kew's site returned a 403 to my automated request, so I used the Edinburgh herbarium instead.

r: The question I keep returning to is the one in the title, and it applies to each object separately. What is meant to continue, and what is meant to hold its form? A growth interval and the time a preserved form stays usable are different measurements. Each belongs on the label next to the intention, with the date of the last observation.

posts.title: How could a clothing manifesto become policy?
posts.subtitle: De Klerenpartij will stage a council meeting in Eindhoven's council chamber on October 23, 2026. Dutch and European law, a neighboring council's paper trail and Eindhoven's own rules show where a clothing motion has to travel to change anything.
posts.seoTitle: How could a clothing manifesto become policy?
posts.description: De Klerenpartij stages a council meeting in Eindhoven on October 23, 2026. Dutch and EU law and a neighboring council's record show how far a motion travels.

r: A clothing manifesto can fit on a banner. A clothing policy has to name who buys what, who pays for it and which law lets them. De Klerenpartij, in the Dutch Design Week 2026 program, will take over Eindhoven's council chamber on Friday, October 23, with speakers, motions, debate and what the program calls a real vote. It also says, in the same text, that it is not a real political party.

I work as a content strategist, and I read a headline for the claim it makes. "Clothing enters the council chamber" describes a place and a performance. "The council adopted a clothing policy" would describe a decision. This essay uses public documents only: the program page, the initiative's own site, Eindhoven's council page, Dutch and European legislation, a Zwolle council paper and a 2024 Eindhoven initiative proposal. It reports no visit and no conversation with the organizers. Where a statement is the initiative's own, I say so.

blocks.x: What the program says will happen

r: The program describes a staged council meeting conducted according to protocol. The chair opens, De Klerenpartij submits its motions, council members ask questions, speakers are heard and then comes the voting.

The meeting runs from 14:30 to 16:00 in the Raadzaal at Stadhuisplein 1, with doors at 14:00 and drinks until 17:00. Admission is free, there are only 100 seats, registration is required and the meeting is held in Dutch. The program also warns that the opening hours shown elsewhere on the page do not apply to this event.

The initiative describes itself as an initiative by Dagan Cohen and Billie van Katwijk, a political movement for a fairer, circular and locally rooted clothing system that uses humor, protest, motions and public council meetings.

Its site says it grew out of a storylab called Reshaping The Fashion Narrative, organized by AMFI and the creative network Changency in June 2025, with more than 45 participants, and that it was launched through a protest performance at the Society 5.0 festival in Amsterdam in October 2025.

blocks.x: The motions already exist, for another city

r: The old version of this essay imagined a hypothetical motion about uniforms. The initiative has since published real ones. On May 21, 2026 it announced that it would submit motions in the council chamber of Arnhem on May 29, during State of Fashion, and it said they were drafted with more than twenty pioneers from the fashion and textile sector.
I did not find published motions for the Eindhoven meeting, so the Arnhem set is the best evidence of what to expect, and it is only that.

Motion 1 asks the council to teach primary pupils to sew, knit and crochet, to let secondary pupils visit the whole textile chain and to make sustainable clothing alternatives visible in the city. Motion 2 asks for affordable space, subsidy and growth programs for circular entrepreneurs and for fair access to prominent locations and subsidized public outdoor advertising. Motion 3 asks the municipality to put circular textile policy into practice inside its own organization: buy only locally made, (bio)circular workwear and interior textiles, work with local repairers, run swap events and repair corners in the town hall and train civil servants.
The page does not say who voted or what the result was, and I found no later record of the outcome.
Motion 3 is the uniform question I had imagined, and it shows why a request is different from an intention.

blocks.x: The manifesto is wider than the motions

r: The initiative's manifesto lists five demands: ban fast fashion advertising, starting with outdoor advertising; make polluters pay through high import tariffs on cheap synthetic textiles and a ban on exporting textile waste; support local clothing production across the circular chain; teach every child sewing, knitting and repairing; and set a fair price and fair chain, with brands paying for collection, repair and recycling.
The manifesto aligns itself with the EU Strategy for Sustainable and Circular Textiles of 2022.
Those demands do not all belong to the same level of government. Sorting them is the quickest way to see what a municipal council can do.

blocks.x: Who holds the power over each demand

r: Brands paying for collection and recycling is already law in the Netherlands. The Besluit uitgebreide producentenverantwoordelijkheid textiel, an extended producer responsibility decree in force since July 1, 2023, covers consumer clothing and business clothing. It requires producers to see that rising shares of what they put on the Dutch market are prepared for reuse or recycled: 50 percent by weight in 2025, rising to 75 percent from 2030, with separate shares for reuse and fiber-to-fiber recycling.
Because it names business clothing, it reaches uniforms and workwear.

The European Union has now generalized the idea. Directive (EU) 2025/1892, signed on September 10, 2025, inserts an extended producer responsibility scheme for textiles into the Waste Framework Directive, with producer costs for collection and waste management, producer responsibility organizations and registers of producers. Member states must bring it into force by June 17, 2027.
It also lets member states modulate producers' fees according to practices linked to ultra-fast and fast fashion, such as product life span and repair incentives.

The directive does not ban exports of used textiles. Its recitals say that separately collected used textiles are to count as waste, and be sorted, before they are shipped, in order to combat illegal shipments.
The tariff demand sits at the EU level too. The Dutch decree itself refers to the common customs tariff, set by Council Regulation (EEC) No 2658/87, as the classification it uses.
A municipal council has no part in customs duties.
That leaves the demands a council can touch: its own purchasing, its schools policy, its support for local businesses and what appears on public advertising space it controls.

blocks.x: Buying only local workwear runs into procurement law

r: Motion 3 would have the municipality buy only locally made, circular workwear. Dutch procurement law, the Aanbestedingswet 2012, says in article 1.8 that a contracting authority treats businesses equally and without discrimination, and in article 1.10 that the requirements it sets must be in reasonable proportion to the subject of the contract.

I am not a procurement specialist, and a rule that only locally made goods may be bought would need that kind of review. On its face it sits uneasily with equal treatment. Circular and repair criteria tied to the contract's subject, such as durability and take-back, look more compatible with the proportionality article. That reading is my own and not a legal opinion.

blocks.x: Advertising: a council tried, in this room

r: The first manifesto demand has a local history. In February 2024 the Partij voor de Dieren, with Volt, GroenLinks and the PvdA, put an initiative proposal to the Eindhoven council to keep advertising for fossil fuels and animal food products out of public space. It proposed talks with advertising operators within six months, a legal study within nine and a regulation within twelve if the study allowed it.
The proposal's own text lists Eindhoven's outdoor advertising contracts, with end dates from December 2029 to December 2032, and says Eindhoven's advertising policy dates from 2010.
The sponsors considered fast fashion and left it out, writing that overconsumption of clothing is a big problem but that clothing consumption cannot reasonably be avoided in the way meat can.

A July 2024 paper to the Zwolle council describes what happened next elsewhere. Zwolle's council had adopted a motion in May 2023 asking for a ban on fossil advertising in its general local bylaw. The executive's reply was that a ban looked legally possible but hard to defend, because advertising is protected as freedom of expression under article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights and any limit needs a pressing social need, proportionality and a basis in law. It noted that a court test and damages claims were possible, estimated monitoring and enforcement at about 60,000 euros a year, and asked why a ban would cover fossil fuels and not fast fashion or meat. It advised the council not to adopt the ban.

The same paper says Eindhoven's council had recently rejected a proposal for a bylaw ban on advertising for meat and air travel because of doubts about feasibility, and that Den Haag and Utrecht were instead banning fossil advertising through new contracts with advertising operators.

That contract route is how Amsterdam appears to have done it. Reporting by VRT NWS on May 4, 2026 says Amsterdam has banned public advertising for fossil fuels and meat, such as flights, cruises, fast-food meat and petrol and diesel cars, while businesses may still advertise at their own shops.
It does not include fast fashion.

So the manifesto's first demand has no precedent in Dutch cities that I could find, and its closest relatives have run into legal doubt, contract terms that end in 2029 or later and a council that has already said no once.

blocks.x: How a motion becomes anything

r: The Vereniging van Nederlandse Gemeenten (VNG) explains that a motion is a proposal for the council to make a statement. It is not a decision aimed at legal effect. It has political and not legal meaning, so the executive is formally not bound by it or obliged to carry it out, although setting it aside can lead to a breach of trust between council and executive.

Eindhoven's council page describes the council as setting the main lines of municipal policy and overseeing the executive. It has 45 members, elected in March 2026 for four years, and a coalition of PRO, CDA and D66.

The page lists how a resident gets a topic in front of it: contact a councillor, speak for five minutes at an opinion-forming meeting on an agenda item, file a petition, or file a citizens' motion or citizens' initiative with at least 250 signatures. A citizens' motion asks for a statement from the council, and a citizens' initiative is a complete proposal on which the council always decides in a council meeting.
A staged vote in the Raadzaal is not on that list. The program does not say who votes. Nothing I read suggests the staged result enters the council's record, and the program does not claim it does.

The real routes are the ones the council describes. The VNG describes motions as submitted by councillors, and I did not read Eindhoven's own rules of order, so I cannot say what else Eindhoven allows.

blocks.x: What to look for after October 23

r: Follow one motion. Which text was submitted, and by whom in the real council? Which law or contract would let the executive act on it? What did it answer, and by when? A motion on workwear leads to procurement files. A motion on advertising leads to concession contracts. A motion on schools leads to a conversation with schools, which I did not research here. Each has a document trail, and the trail is shorter than the manifesto.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: The text of any motion for the Eindhoven meeting, and who votes in the staged vote.
The outcome of the Arnhem vote on May 29, 2026, and whether any council took up the motions.
Whether the Eindhoven council or any real councillor has received a motion from the initiative.
The exact council decisions of May 2024 on advertising. I rely on Zwolle's account that Eindhoven rejected the proposal, and the proposal's own text.
How Amsterdam's advertising ban is legally built. I have only press reporting.
Whether the procurement-law reading above would hold for a specific purchase.
How school curricula, which Motion 1 touches, are governed. I did not research it.

r: The question for a reader leaving the chamber is the one in the title, made concrete. Which sentence in the manifesto could a named official act on next Monday, under which law, and who would check?

posts.title: An independent practice still needs other people
posts.subtitle: LABOUR! at Dutch Design Week 2026 asks architects and designers to treat precarious work as a shared problem. European competition law, a 2015 Dutch cao experiment and the architecture sector's new collective agreement show how far a freelancer can organize.
posts.seoTitle: An independent practice still needs other people
posts.description: LABOUR! at Dutch Design Week 2026 treats precarious design work as a shared problem. What EU and Dutch competition rules and a new cao say about freelancers.

r: Independent work is a feeling and a legal status, and the law has decided that in some situations the two do not match. Self-employed architects who earn 90 percent of their income from one firm may, according to the European Commission, negotiate working conditions with that firm together, and a competition rule that normally forbids rivals from agreeing prices does not stand in the way. The Commission uses almost exactly that example in its own guidelines.

LABOUR! and the Strength of a Union gives the question a place in the Dutch Design Week 2026 program. Netherlands Angry Architects (NAA!) built it with the trade union federation FNV for the Klokgebouw on Strijp-S, and describes it as an installation that works as an exhibition, archive, meeting point and temporary workers' assembly.

This essay uses public documents only: the program page, a fellowship profile of the collective, the Commission's guidelines, the competition authority's pages, a 2015 news report and a union announcement from August 2026. It reports no meeting, no interview and no visit, and it speaks for none of the participants.

blocks.x: What the exhibition says it is

r: The program says the installation looks at labor conditions, collective organizing and solidarity in architecture and the wider creative sector, among architects, designers, cultural workers and builders working in industries "increasingly shaped by precarity, unpaid overtime, individual negotiation and invisible labour." It says the project asks workers to see these conditions as shared structural issues and not as individual struggles.

Built from scaffold elements, mesh panels, concrete blocks and timber, it hosts testimonies, labor statistics, workers' rights material and collective research, with a central table for discussions and workshops. Visitors are invited to contribute testimonies and connect with others, and the program says it links trade-union networks with grassroots groups, including those united through Architectural Workers International.

NAA! describes itself as a collective that organizes architectural workers around fair labor, transparency and worker-led governance. According to the program it was initiated in 2022 with the support of Failed Architecture and FNV and works through a "workers inquiry" approach: public workers-only meetings, ad hoc advice, reports, explainers and live discussions.

A 2024 fellowship profile lists its team as Charlie Clemoes, Anna Mańka and Hazal Su and states its aim as improving working conditions in architecture and design, with attention to workers at the start of their careers and to immigrants and Dutch people with an immigrant background, who it says often face short-term contracts, low wages and limited benefits.
Those are the collective's own descriptions.

The exhibition's claims about unpaid overtime and precarity are claims. I did not find a published survey with figures behind them, and I did not find the workers' inquiry reports the program mentions. Several people describing unpaid revisions can identify something worth investigating. Saying how widespread it is would need a defined group and a method.

blocks.x: Independent in law is not one thing

r: Competition law treats a solo self-employed person as a business. Businesses may not agree prices with one another, and the same rule has been read to cover a freelancer's collective rate. The Commission's 2022 guidelines on collective agreements for solo self-employed persons describe the exceptions. A collective agreement on working conditions falls outside the ban on cartels when the solo self-employed are in a situation comparable to that of workers. The Commission lists three groups: those economically dependent on one counterparty, those who work side by side with employees for the same counterparty, and those who work through digital labor platforms.

For the first group the Commission gives a number. A solo self-employed person is economically dependent where she earns, on average, at least 50 percent of her work-related income from one counterparty over one or two years.

The guidelines then give a worked example. A firm of architects contracts many self-employed architects, who earn 90 percent of their income from it and negotiate together a cap of 45 working hours a week, 26 calendar days of annual leave and rates by experience level. The guidelines say the agreement falls outside Article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, because the architects are economically dependent.

The Dutch competition authority, the ACM, describes the position at home. Its page for freelancers lists four situations in which they may agree rates or conditions, or in which the authority would not fine them: to secure a social minimum, as a very small group or market share (at most eight freelancers with joint annual turnover of at most 1.1 million euros, or at most 10 percent of the market and no effect on trade between EU countries), when they work on assignment but resemble employees, and when the agreement benefits customers more than it harms competition.

A 2017 ACM publication, updated in February 2023 when the authority issued a revised guide, says that minimum rates for freelancers in collective labor agreements are usually not allowed, because price agreements between businesses fall under the cartel ban, and that the exception covers false self-employed people who have less freedom than freelancers to decide where, when and how they work. It credited the European court's ruling on substitute musicians in orchestras with making that exception.

None of this is legal advice. The point is narrower. Whether an independent practice may organize depends on facts about the practice, such as how many customers it has, who directs the work and who sits beside it, and the law names those facts.

blocks.x: The architecture sector tried it in 2015

r: This is not abstract for architecture. On July 20, 2015, NOS reported that the new collective agreement for architecture firms allowed self-employed architects hired by firms to ask for a minimum rate comparable to what an employee architect earns, plus a surcharge for disability insurance, holiday saving and pension. The rule of thumb, according to Victor Frequin of the trade association BNA, was that comparable work should be paid comparably, and that the sector did not want abuse of the large supply of freelancers.

NOS gave the context. The financial crisis had shrunk the sector, from more than 14,500 architects, technical draftspeople and specification writers in 2008 to 6,500. The share of self-employed rose from 6 percent the year before to 16 percent of the total.

Reactions split. A self-employed engineer was glad of a floor to point to when talking to a customer. ZZP Nederland, an organization for freelancers, called the rate counterproductive, said a minimum becomes the norm, and objected that freelancers had not been at the table. NOS noted that it was unclear whether the provision would stand under competition law, and that the ACM did not yet know whether the prohibition applied.
Two years later the ACM's statement said collective parties may not make rate agreements for freelancers in a collective agreement, except where the freelancers are in the employee-like situation.
I did not find what became of the 2015 architecture provision, or whether any freelancer-rate clause survives in the sector's agreement today.

blocks.x: The employees' agreement, signed two months before the show

r: The sector's current collective agreement covers employees. On August 26, 2026, FNV reported that a large majority of its members at architecture firms had accepted the employers' final offer, making the new agreement for 2026 to 2028 definitive. It runs two years from July 1, 2026, and is a minimum agreement, so employer and employee can agree better terms.

FNV's summary lists automatic compensation for inflation capped at 4 percent a year, a pension premium held at 22.8 percent, internship allowances rising on January 1, 2027 to 500 euros a month for vocational students and 650 euros for higher-education students, and 248 vacation hours a year.

Two items bear directly on the exhibition's themes. At FNV's initiative, the parties agreed to work out the rules on overtime and the internship scheme, with the aim of preventing abuse of internships, and FNV says it will keep working on structural overtime, internship abuse and works-council strength.

Those are FNV's statements about what it will pursue. They show that the topics LABOUR! names are on a union's bargaining list, and they also show the limit: the agreement binds employers and employees, and a freelancer is outside it unless one of the exceptions above applies.

blocks.x: Sharing a question is different from sharing a case

r: FNV runs a service for freelancers, which its public page describes as a package for people with their own business, with routes to ask about work, income and membership.

The page does not say who is eligible for what, and it makes no promise about outcomes. That boundary is useful. It tells a reader where a specific conversation could start, and it leaves the organization to state its present terms.

An organizing space also needs readable rules: who may attend, whether a meeting is recorded, what may leave the room and who decides if an account is anonymous. The program describes the central table as open to discussions and says visitors may contribute testimonies, and it does not say how testimonies are handled.
I would want that answered before treating any display of testimony as evidence about a profession.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: How many people the workers' inquiry reached, what it asked and what it found.
Any figures for unpaid overtime or unpaid revisions in Dutch architecture.
How testimonies and meetings at the exhibition are handled.
Whether the 2015 freelancer minimum-rate clause was ever applied, and what replaced it.
The text of the 2026 to 2028 agreement beyond FNV's summary, and the protocol outcome on overtime.
Whether any exhibited testimony concerns freelancers who would meet the Commission's economic-dependence test.

r: The question the title asks has a practical form.

If you work independently, which of your customers holds more than half your income, who directs your hours and who works beside you? The answers decide whether the law treats you as a business or as someone who may bargain together.
