posts.title: Who gets credit for a new material?
posts.subtitle: A close read of the credits on two Dutch Design Week 2026 program pages, an 1858 anatomy title page, and the standards that say what a credit line can and cannot carry.
posts.seoTitle: Who gets credit for a new material?
posts.description: A close read of the credits on two Dutch Design Week 2026 program pages, an 1858 anatomy title page, and the standards behind credit lines.

r: The Dutch Design Week program page for SOW HEMP! lists 32 credits that belong to 30 people, and it still leaves the most interesting question about the show's yarn unanswered.

I read credits the way I read a figure legend, as a claim about who did what. This essay looks at how that claim is made in four places: the SOW HEMP! page from Prague's UMPRUM, the Biomaterials Library page and its own website, a Dutch museum's hemp sample cabinet, and an 1858 anatomy textbook. It then checks what the written standards for credit (a research taxonomy, a photo-metadata standard, a Creative Commons guide, a Dutch copyright statute) say a credit can carry. It uses published pages only. It reports no visit and no interview, and Dutch Design Week itself runs October 17 to 25, 2026, so nothing here describes the exhibits in the room.

blocks.x: One page, thirty people, ten kinds of contribution

r: SOW HEMP! is hosted by UMPRUM, the Academy of Arts, Architecture and Design in Prague, and sits in the Klokgebouw on Strijp-S, with opening hours of 11:00 to 18:00 each day.

The page states its subject plainly. The Studio of Textile explores both the cultural context and the material qualities of hemp fibers, and students worked with hemp yarn, fibers and shives in processes the page lists: dissolving fiber into bioplastic, felting, spinning and carding hemp with wool, tapestry weaving, and fusing raw fibers with a digital embroidery machine.

The colophon is where the credit work happens. It has ten headings. Two staff pairs share the concept and pedagogical guidance, one for the Studio of Textile (Linda Kaplanova and Martin Pondelicek) and one for the Studio of Photography II (Alena Kotzmannova and Tomas Zumr). Exhibition design, text, graphic design and public relations each name two people. Typeface and production name one each. Ten students are listed as exhibiting from the textile studio and eight from the photography studio.

That is 32 entries. Two names appear twice: Tereza Hlavackova is credited with exhibition design and as an exhibiting textile student, and Natalie Mala is credited with graphic design and as an exhibiting textile student.
So the count of people is 30, not 32, and a reader who counts lines gets the wrong number.

The page prints names without Czech diacritics, and I follow its spelling here. That is not a trivial point. UMPRUM's own 2024 page for a different Dutch Design Week show spells one student Zuzana Kotrbová, while the 2026 DDW page prints Zuzana Kotrbova.
Both are plausibly the same person; neither page says so, and I did not check. The difference shows how a credit can shift between two official pages without anyone intending a change.

The image captions follow a second convention. Each names the work, then the maker, then a separate photographer: The Hemp Bag by Anna Sipova (photo Emma Lea Nikodymova), Hyakinthos by Ferdinand Placak (photo Emma Lea Nikodymova), Modulus/Threadline by Simon Leffler and Martin Vorac (photo Maria Michopulu and Jasmina Zivcova), You Are My Star by Natalie Mala (photo Jan Cestr) and Joy by Tereza Hlavackova (photo Maria Michopulu).
The page prints "c)" between each title and the maker's name, and the copy of the same listing at site.ddw.nl prints the same "c)" and adds a copyright sign before the photographer's line.
The photographers named are four of the eight students listed under the Studio of Photography II.
So the photographer is also a member of the exhibition team, which the caption format does not show on its face. The page does not say what the other four photography students exhibit.

blocks.x: What the page names only in passing

r: The page tells a processing story and credits very little of it by name. It says that hemp fiber is not processed for the textile industry in the Czech Republic, and that one farm built scutching machinery from scratch to get short hemp fibers.
The farm is not named anywhere on the page, in the colophon or in the captions.

It then describes a piece of research with the weaving mill Kubák to see whether a local hemp and wool blend could become an industrial yarn, and says the resulting yarn, made by a local weaving mill, met the qualities needed for architecture and interior design.

The mill is named once, in prose, and not in the colophon. The page does not say who ran the research, who spun the blend, in what proportion, or whether the local weaving mill of the second sentence is the Kubák of the first. It reads as the same mill, but that is a reading.

UMPRUM handled the same mill differently in 2024. For its wool show VLNA, shown at Dutch Design Week from October 19 to 27, 2024, the studio's page ends with a separate line of thanks for cooperation that names the Faculty of Textile Engineering at the Technical University of Liberec, an individual (Linda Havrlíková), and Weaving factory Kubák Strmilov, k.s.
That page also splits roles into exhibitors, pedagogical leadership, graphic design, installation concept, curatorial text and photography, with a partner (ČEZ Group) named after the credits.

So the studio has a credit vocabulary that can hold a supplier. The 2026 DDW page uses a template with a fixed set of fields, and a mill that is not one of the fields appears only if the text mentions it.

Kubák is a family weaving workshop in Strmilov, in South Bohemia. A Forbes Czech feature published June 8, 2016 says the first workshop was founded there in 1870, that the family still weaves on looms from the 1930s, and that it makes wool blankets and throws.
I mention this only because it shows what a one-line credit leaves out: a mill with more than 150 years of its own history reduced to a name in a sentence.

blocks.x: A studio that has credited a collective before

r: UMPRUM's textile studio has a documented history of work with no single author. In June and July 2025 the university's gallery showed Individual, Collective, an exhibition curated by Veronika Soukupova and Marketa Vinglerova about the Textile Arts Studio, built around a monumental tapestry made in 1965 through the collaborative effort of all the studio's students under Antonin Kybal.

The gallery page says the tapestry, Natural Wealth of the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic, went well beyond the usual scope of a student project, that it was woven only in natural shades of sheep's wool, and that the account of its making was reconstructed from photographs in the studio's albums and from the memories of graduates.
Its closing acknowledgments thank the textile artists who contributed to the tapestry as a group, not by name.

I do not draw a line from that exhibition to the 2026 colophon. A Veronika Soukupova is credited for text on the SOW HEMP! page; the name matches, and I have no evidence either way about whether it is the same person.

What the 2025 page does show is that the institution is aware of the problem. A collective piece produced a record in which individual contribution had to be recovered from photographs and oral recollection sixty years later, and the exhibition made that recovery its subject.

blocks.x: The title page that ranked its contributors

r: Anatomy is the field I know best, and its illustrated books have always carried this question on the title page. The first edition of Henry Gray's Anatomy, Descriptive and Surgical, published in London by John W. Parker and Son in 1858, reads in a Royal College of Surgeons library catalog record: the drawings by H. V. Carter, M.D., late Demonstrator of Anatomy at St. George's Hospital, and the dissections jointly by the author and Dr. Carter.
A Wellcome Collection record for a digitized copy carries the same wording.
The catalog lists Carter in a separate field as illustrator.

The text splits what people usually bundle. Gray is the author. Carter made 363 drawings, per the Linda Hall Library, and the title page says the dissections were made jointly by the author and Carter.
The author's preface thanks Carter and says all the drawings from which the engravings were made were executed by him, in most cases copied from or corrected by dissections made jointly.
That is a contribution described with verbs, on the page where a reader would meet it, and nothing about it was hidden.

The surrounding record is less comfortable. The Linda Hall Library says Gray sent back the title-page proofs and demanded that the size of Carter's name be reduced and his titles removed, and that in most modern editions Carter's name does not appear.

Hektoen International, in a 2025 biography, reports some evidence that Gray emphasized Carter's secondary role, even insisting on a smaller type size, and says Gray received a royalty of 150 pounds for every 1,000 copies while Carter received a single fee of 150 pounds.
The two accounts disagree about the titles. The cataloged title page settles that point: it prints Carter's degree and his hospital post.
Whether the type was reduced cannot be read from a transcription, and I did not see the copies. The claim about modern editions rests on the Linda Hall account alone.

The lesson for a material story is narrow. Credit has at least three layers: what a text says, how big the name is, and what the money did. The same page can credit generously in words and still rank people in type and contract. A published colophon shows the first layer only.

blocks.x: What the standards say a credit can carry

r: Four written sources describe different parts of the job, and none covers all of it.
CRediT, the Contributor Role Taxonomy, is a community-owned list of 14 contributor roles approved in 2022 as an ANSI/NISO standard and licensed CC BY 4.0.
Its roles include conceptualization, methodology, investigation, resources, supervision, project administration, visualization and two kinds of writing.
The maintainers state that it is not designed to determine authorship, and that it can be used to describe contributions in contexts other than article authorship.

It was built for research papers, so its words (investigation, validation) fit a lab better than a textile studio, but its idea carries: a role is a verb, not a rank. The SOW HEMP! page uses nouns such as text and production, which tell you the category of work but not the extent of it.

The IPTC Photo Metadata Standard separates three things most captions merge. Creator is the photographer's name; Credit Line is the credit the supplier requires to be shown when the image is published; and Copyright Notice identifies the copyright owner.
IPTC adds that metadata stripped from images by a publishing system can infringe on the copyright holders' rights and may be illegal in some countries.
A photo credit therefore has a structured home. Whether the DDW press-kit images carry that metadata is something I did not check.

Creative Commons asks reusers of licensed work to give Title, Author, Source and License (TASL), and says the form of attribution should be reasonable for the medium and should follow the licensor's request about how to be named.
Dutch Design Week gives its own rule for its photo library: always credit Dutch Design Week and the photographer.
Those are different instructions for different material, and a story that uses both needs both.

The Dutch Copyright Act adds a legal layer. In the unofficial English translation by Mireille van Eechoud of the University of Amsterdam, which reflects the Act as in force on January 1, 2012 and needs checking against the current text, Article 4 presumes the maker to be the person named as maker in or on the work.

Article 5 says that for a work made of separate works, the person who directed and supervised it is taken as maker of the whole, without prejudice to the copyright in each separate work. Article 7 treats an employer as the maker of works made in service, unless otherwise agreed. Article 8 treats an organization that makes a work public as its own, without naming a natural person, as its maker.
Article 25(1)(a) lets a maker oppose publication of the work without mention of the maker's name, unless opposition would be unreasonable, and Article 25(3) says that right may be waived.

Which country's law applies to a Czech student's work shown in the Netherlands is a separate question I cannot answer, and I draw no conclusion about any SOW HEMP! participant. I use the statute to make one point: a name on a work is evidence about who made it, and neither proof of authorship nor a contract.

blocks.x: Two different ways to name a maker

r: The Biomaterials Library gives a second pattern. Its About page says it is the first publicly accessible physical collection of its kind in the Baltic States, based in Vilnius and expanding online, founded and curated by Austėja Platūkytė, organized by the NGO Medžiagotyra and supported by the Lithuanian Council for Culture.

Those are three roles (curator, organizer, funder) written in a single closing block, each with a different verb. The About page also says materials are presented through their sources, transformation processes, properties, applications and end-of-life pathways.
On the Library's own site, each material page ends with a single Created by line. Giria is created by Evelina Kudabaite, and Pine Skins by Studio Sarmīte.
Amber Waste Is Bliss is created by Studio Agne, and Vegetative Textiles by Indre Spitryte.
Waste Matters is created by Waste Matters, with a studio website named.

The text of each page describes process in some detail. Giria, for example, describes collecting bark waste from sawmills, drying, grinding, sieving, boiling a binder and molding, and notes that no two items are the same.

The DDW listing for the Library's Dutch Design Week 2026 exhibition, hosted at BioArt Laboratories in the Strijp T+R area with free access, names the makers in captions with the copyright sign: Indrė Spitrytė-Mikuckė for Vegetative Textiles, Waste Matters Studio for Coffee Waste Tiles, Evelina Kudabaitė for Giria and Sarmite Polakova for Pine Skins. Its lead caption gives Agnė Kučerenkaitė for Amber Waste is Bliss.
Its colophon has one entry, the founder and curator, who is also the curator of the exhibition.
Set the two sets of names side by side and the problem becomes visible. Pine Skins is credited to "Studio Sarmīte" on the Library's page and to "Sarmite Polakova" on the DDW page.
Amber Waste Is Bliss is "Studio Agne" on one and "Agnė Kučerenkaitė" on the other.
Even a single maker's name changes between the two sites: Evelina Kudabaite on the Library's page, Evelina Kudabaitė on the DDW listing.

The studio-name pairs are most likely the same people under a studio name and a personal name. I cannot confirm that from the pages, and a story that picks one version should ask the maker which form they prefer before it prints either. The Textielmuseum cabinet shows the opposite case, two lines that stay distinct.

blocks.x: A cabinet with two lines

r: The Textielmuseum in Tilburg published photographs of its textile sample cabinet on Wikimedia Commons. An October 6, 2026 read of the file page for the hemp tray (Textielmuseum-cabinet-12) recorded the photographer as Joep Vogels, the date as April 29, 2011, the cabinet interior as the work of Simone de Waart of Material Sense, and the license as CC BY-SA 4.0.

I did not reopen that page for this version, so the reading is as recorded in October. Two lines, two jobs: one for the interior, one for the photograph, and a license line that governs reuse and is separate from both.

The museum's own page for its library returned an HTTP 403 when I tried it, so I could not check the credit against the museum's wording. One more limit follows from the photograph itself. It shows the hemp tray of a cabinet that holds many fibers, and the interior credit belongs to the cabinet, so neither line says who made or supplied the samples in the tray.

blocks.x: Keeping the names when a story gets short

r: A magazine caption can hold a full credit. A vertical video may show an object for three seconds. The standards above point to a practical answer: keep a record for each image, written once, with the object's maker in the exact spelling they use, a verb for each contribution, the photographer, the image owner, the license or permission, and the date. IPTC gives the photographer and credit line their own fields, CC gives the attribution elements, and the DDW image library asks for the photographer by name.

An article can then explain how the collaboration worked, when the reporting supports it. A short video can carry a readable on-screen maker credit and a fuller description. A multi-slide post can place each credit on its own slide. These are proposed practices. I describe no internal approval process at UMPRUM, at the Library or at Dutch Design Week, and I do not claim any of them needs fixing.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: The SOW HEMP! page does not name the farm that built the scutching machinery. It does not say who led the Kubák research, what the blend contained, or whether the mill that made the yarn is the same Kubák named in the preceding sentence.
It does not say whether the exhibiting students' individual works use the Kubák yarn.
Neither the DDW press-kit images nor the Library's website images state a license in the pages I read, so the credit lines do not tell a reader what reuse is allowed.
I did not check the images' embedded metadata. The Textielmuseum reading is as recorded on October 6, 2026 and was not repeated.
The Dutch Act translation reflects 2012, and the current wording may differ.
The Gray and Carter material rests on a library catalog entry, a medical-history article and a library's science-history post, and I did not see a physical copy of the title page.
Nothing here is a finding that anyone was under-credited. The pages I read show how credit is structured and where it thins. They do not show any dispute among the participants, and I know of none.

The question I would take to the exhibition is the plainest one. For any object, ask the maker who else should be named and what that person did, and write the answer down in the maker's words before the headline gets written.

posts.title: What a photograph still cannot explain
posts.subtitle: Rules from photojournalism, web accessibility and photo metadata, plus one psychology experiment, on what a caption has to carry that the picture cannot.
posts.seoTitle: What a photograph still cannot explain
posts.description: What World Press Photo, W3C and IPTC rules say a caption must carry that a picture cannot, with one experiment on how photos inflate belief.

r: In a 2012 experiment, university students who saw a photograph beside a claim were more likely to judge the claim true, even though the photograph said nothing about whether it was.

That result is the reason I keep asking what a picture of a material, a screen or a maker is actually evidence of. This essay sets out what four sets of published rules say a photograph must be paired with: the World Press Photo contest's caption and verification requirements, the W3C's guidance on text alternatives, the IPTC photo metadata standard, and the Dutch Copyright Act's provisions on portraits. It uses published sources only. It reports no visit, no interview and no photographs of my own, and Dutch Design Week itself runs October 17 to 25, 2026.

blocks.x: A picture can raise confidence without adding evidence

r: Newman and four co-authors ran four experiments, published in Psychonomic Bulletin and Review in 2012. In the first two, people saw celebrity names and quickly answered true or false to either "This famous person is alive" or "This famous person is dead." For some names a photograph of the celebrity at work appeared too. For unfamiliar names, the photograph made people more likely to say the claim was true, and it did so for both the alive claim and the dead claim, so the effect was a pull toward true rather than toward alive.
The authors also tested words. A short verbal description of the celebrity produced a similar effect, so the paper does not say photographs are special.

A third experiment used general-knowledge trivia, with 70 students, and found that a photograph related to the subject of a statement but silent on its truth nudged people toward calling the statement true, most clearly for the hard statements.
The authors suggest, without settling it, that both photos and words help people generate pseudo-evidence for the claim they are reading.

The limits are real. The subjects were university students, the judgments were made in seconds, and the claims were trivia. The paper does not test a museum label or a magazine caption. I read it as a narrow warning: a picture placed next to a sentence can make the sentence feel more supported than it is. A caption that says what the picture does not show works against that.

blocks.x: What a prize-winning photograph is required to say about itself

r: World Press Photo has written down more of this than most publishers. For the 2026 contest, captions must answer who, what, where, when and why. The short description has to say who is in the photograph and what is going on, name the place, and give the date. Actions not seen must be attributed to a source, and the long description must explain the circumstances in which the picture was taken. If the photographer influenced the scene or directed a subject to pose, that must be disclosed. Information about consent belongs in the caption.

The contest also checks. Entries are screened against the rules. Entrants whose photographs progress must supply the file as recorded by the camera: a RAW file, or full-format JPEGs as delivered by the camera in a series of at least seven frames (three before the entry, the entry itself and three after), or the equivalent for smartphones and film. Two independent digital analysts compare the originals with the entries. After the winners are chosen, an external research team checks, among other things, whether the persons named in a caption are in the photo, whether an event happened, whether a depicted animal is the species named, and whether the place and date are right.

The contest's stated reason is that it rewards photographs that are visual documents giving an accurate and fair representation of the scene the photographer witnessed, and that it does not want prize-winning photographs to mislead the audience.
It dates its first manipulation rule to 2009, the requirement to supply original camera files to 2014, and the current rules and processes to a revision for the 2016 contest.

None of this means a museum or a design festival should copy a press-photo rulebook. It shows what a serious standard asks beside the image: a date, a place, a named person who can be checked, a statement of what was arranged, and a source for anything the camera could not see. The seven-frame requirement carries a second lesson. The frames before and after a picture are evidence about it, and a single frame may hide what the neighbors would reveal.

blocks.x: Four jobs that are easy to merge

r: The IPTC Photo Metadata User Guide separates fields that publishers often collapse. Description/Caption tells the who, what, and possibly where, when and why of what is happening in the photograph. Alt Text is a brief description of the purpose and meaning of the image for assistive technology and for when the image is not displayed, and the guide says the two should not be confused. Extended Description is for more detail and should not repeat the alt text. Date Created records when the image was created and can be derived from the camera's Exif date. A separate Date Created field for the artwork or object shows when the thing photographed was made.

The W3C's guidance sets the logic for alt text: an informative image needs a text alternative that conveys its essential information, a decorative image should have an empty one, and a complex image needs a short description plus a long one. It adds that the author must decide the text alternative from the usage, context and content of the image.
The success criterion behind it, WCAG 2.2 criterion 1.1.1, asks for a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.

"Equivalent purpose" is the phrase that matters for this essay. If the reason a photograph is in an article is to show a difference between two samples, a description that says "two samples on a table" has not done its job.

The state of the web suggests how often this fails. The WebAIM Million analysis of one million home pages, run in February 2026, found missing alternative text on 53.1% of home pages; 16.2% of all home-page images lacked it, and 10.8% of images with alternative text had questionable or repetitive text such as a file name.
Those figures describe popular websites, not design journalism. They are a reminder that the default is an unexplained picture.

blocks.x: Three dates, and a sample that keeps changing

r: A photograph has at least three dates attached to it. One is when it was made. The second is when the object in it was made, which IPTC tracks in its own field. The third is when the page describing it was last updated.
A crop for a social post can drop all three.

Dutch Design Week's own image library shows what a basic record contains. Each entry in the press image library lists a date, an area of the city or a venue name, and a photographer, for example an October 18, 2025 entry at Ketelhuisplein by Max Kneefel, and the page asks users to always credit Dutch Design Week and the photographer.
That is a date, a place and a credit. It does not say what a viewer is looking at beyond the venue name, and it does not say anything about a version.

Materials make the gap wider. The Biomaterials Library's Dutch Design Week page says its collection preserves different stages of material development, from early tests and samples to refined applications and design objects, and that each material carries knowledge about its ingredients, processes, failures and possibilities.

A photograph of two samples can't say which is the early test. The Library's own page for the Giria homeware collection adds a time dimension: it says the collection's materials may change slowly over time, that objects deform as they dry, mostly depending on thickness, and that no two items are the same.
A picture of one Giria bowl is a picture of one object at one point in its drying and aging.

blocks.x: Composition and process: what a clean surface leaves out

r: The Library's page for Amber Waste Is Bliss gives a different example. It says the biocomposites combine natural amber dust with other reclaimed materials, that the pieces are made with a heat press in a non-oxygen environment, that cellulose from sewage waste and the solid remains of hemp after oil extraction are added to counter softness and brittleness, and that the composites carry more than 50 percent amber dust.

A photograph of a finished tile can show color, finish and edge. It cannot show the percentage, the process or the additives. Those claims come from the maker's page, and a caption that repeats them should say so. The page also gives two temperatures for the resin, a melting temperature of around 150 degrees Celsius and a start of melting at 250 to 300 degrees, without reconciling them in the text I read.
A caption writer who meets that kind of inconsistency has to ask the maker, and a picture will not settle it.

The same logic applies to motion, screens and models. A clip of a sample bending shows the action in the clip; it does not by itself establish durability, repeatability or fitness for a product. A screen showing a link between an organization and a service might be a measurement, a classification or an illustration. World Press Photo's rule that actions not seen need attribution is a workable template: say who says so.

blocks.x: Not every picture is a capture

r: A photograph from a phone is already a processed image. IPTC's Digital Source Type vocabulary, first added to the standard in 2008 and extended in 2022 and 2024 as generative AI spread, separates an original digital capture from a multi-frame computational capture, which it describes as several frames merged automatically, including the HDR processing common in smartphone camera apps.
The same list has terms for screen captures, virtual event recordings, composites of captured elements, human-edited media, media edited using generative AI and media created using generative AI.
The list exists because a viewer cannot tell these apart by looking.

For an exhibit, that matters in two ways. A screenshot of a simulation is a record of what a screen displayed, which is different from a record of an event. And a concept image supplied by an exhibitor may be a rendering. A caption that states the source type, in plain words, does the same job as the metadata field: it says what kind of picture this is before anyone asks what it shows.

blocks.x: People in the frame

r: Faces are the place where a caption is most tempted to explain too much. A maker who looks pleased beside an object has not told the camera they are satisfied with the result, and a person pausing during an activity has not shown that they are confused. A caption can record what a person says, with permission, and attribute it. World Press Photo's captions guidance asks for consent information to appear in the caption.
IPTC has a field for the names of persons shown in an image.

The Dutch Copyright Act has its own rules about portraits. In the unofficial English translation by Mireille van Eechoud, which reflects the Act as in force on January 1, 2012, Article 21 says that if a portrait was made without a commission from the person portrayed, the copyright owner may not make it public where the person portrayed has a reasonable interest against publication.

A Dutch law firm's explainer describes the structure around it: portraits made on commission fall under Articles 19 and 20, where publication in principle needs the portrayed person's consent; portraits made without commission, which it calls by far the most common case, may in principle be published freely unless a reasonable interest, such as privacy or an exploitation interest, stands against it; and the General Data Protection Regulation may apply separately.

I cite this to show that a face in a frame raises a question the photograph cannot answer, namely whether the person has an interest against publication. It is not a legal conclusion about any photograph. The translation's wording of Article 20 does not match the law firm's description of it, so the official Dutch text needs checking before anyone relies on either.

blocks.x: A record that survives the crop

r: The seven-frame rule, the caption fields and the alt-text guidance suggest a record that can be kept for each picture at the moment it is made. It would hold the identifier the exhibitor uses for the object, the version or date the account applies to, the maker's name in the form they use, the photographer, the context frame the detail belongs to, and the question the picture is meant to help answer.
Two checks follow from the standards. Read the article without the image, and see whether the reason for the comparison is still clear; that is the W3C test of equivalent purpose.

Then look at the image with only its caption, and see whether the caption blocks the most likely misreading; that is what the World Press Photo fact-checkers do when they ask whether the caption matches the scene.
Where a field is empty, record the gap as a question with a name on it, for example the composition claim that needs the maker's page as its source.

A short example shows the idea, with the sentence below written as a hypothetical caption for a picture that does not exist. "A bowl from the Giria collection by Evelina Kudabaite. The Biomaterials Library's page says the collection is made by hand from tree-bark dust, coated with food-safe oils, and that no two items are alike; the photograph shows this bowl on the date it was taken and not its later state." The first sentence identifies the object and maker. The second attributes every claim about material and process to the page and says what the picture is a record of. A reader can check each part.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: The Newman experiment tested students on trivia and celebrity names, and it does not measure what a caption does to a reader of a design article.
The World Press Photo rules apply to a photojournalism contest, and I have not seen any rule from Dutch Design Week about captions beyond its instruction to credit the photographer.
The IPTC User Guide describes what the fields are for; I did not check which of them the Dutch Design Week press images carry.
The WebAIM figures describe home pages, not newsletters.
The Dutch Copyright Act translation is a 2012 snapshot with a passage that conflicts with a secondary source, and the law firm explainer is not dated.

The question I would carry into any exhibit with a camera is what the picture will be asked to prove after it leaves the room, and whether the caption can say, in one sentence a stranger could check, what it does not.

posts.title: Where does the captured pollution go next?
posts.subtitle: VENTRA, a student-built electric concept car, catches tire dust at the wheel. European rules, a Dutch emissions estimate and a London start-up's own results show what comes after the catch, and what is still not documented.
posts.seoTitle: Where does the captured pollution go next?
posts.description: VENTRA catches tire dust at the wheel. What Euro 7, EU waste law, a Dutch estimate and a London start-up say about what happens next.

r: The numbers attached to VENTRA are 24 percent and 42 percent, and both come from simulation: the team's project page attributes them to simulations, and a design magazine's report says the figures come from simulations and that street testing will be more telling.

I keep returning to a simpler question that no figure answers. When someone opens the collection surface and empties it, where does the dust go? This essay follows that question through the team's own pages, the European Union's Euro 7 regulation, the EU's waste directive, a Dutch government institute's tire-wear estimate and the published results of a London company that works on the same problem. It uses public sources only. It reports no road test, no visit and no interview, and Dutch Design Week itself runs October 17 to 25, 2026.

blocks.x: What VENTRA is, in its makers' words

r: The Dutch Design Week 2026 program lists TU/ecomotive VENTRA as an exhibition at the Klokgebouw on Strijp-S, hosted by TU/ecomotive Team EM-11, with a DDW ticket required.

The listing calls it a lightweight electric concept car engineered to capture particulate matter directly from its own tires and brakes. It says the onboard T.R.A.C.E. system uses electrostatic precipitation to draw fine particles from the wheels with minimal aerodynamic drag, that the carbon-fiber mainframe weighs 45.5 kilograms and the whole chassis 135, and that visitors can see the two-seater with its doors open and orange wheel caps marking the capture zones.
The team describes itself as a student group from Eindhoven University of Technology that builds a new concept car every year, with VENTRA its eleventh, made by 43 students from 23 nationalities.

The team's own overview page lists the cars by year from Penny in 2013 to VENTRA in 2026, and says it builds a vehicle roughly every one to one and a half years with about 30 students from eight academic disciplines.
The counts do not agree: the listing says 43 students, the overview page gives about 30 as the team's usual size, and a news report says VENTRA was developed by 40.
The listing is the team's own submission to the festival, so I use its figure and note the others.

The project page names three steps: reduce, monitor and capture. The vehicle weighs 790 kilograms with an estimated WLTP range of 290 kilometers. A carbon-fiber-reinforced thermoplastic chassis keeps weight off the tires. A feedback system called Clean Drive reads steering, braking and acceleration data and suggests changes that cause less wear. T.R.A.C.E. charges the released particles and draws them onto collection surfaces.
The team says a comparable chassis built by traditional methods would weigh about 230 kilograms.
Its own press page describes the car as the electric car that captures the particles its own tires leave behind.

blocks.x: What the percentages describe

r: The project page says simulations show that between 50 and 80 kilometers per hour more than 24 percent of the particles released by the tires are routed into the collection system, and that in slower city driving fans draw air in and lift the captured share to 42 percent.
A design-magazine report of the car repeats both figures and adds that they come from simulations, so testing on real streets will be the more telling next stage.
A news report on the September 30, 2026 unveiling gives 42 percent at lower urban speeds and 24 percent at 50 to 80 kilometers per hour.

Two details narrow what those numbers can mean. First, the project page states them for tire particles. The festival listing says the car captures matter from its tires and brakes, and the news and design coverage say T.R.A.C.E. pulls both from the air, but the quantified claim I found is about tires.

Second, a capture share needs a denominator. The page does not say whether the share is by mass or by number, which particle sizes it counts, or whether the particles "released by the tires" include the coarse ones that fall to the road.
A modeled share entering a collector says little about exposure to someone walking beside the road.

The Dutch national picture shows why the denominator matters. A 2016 RIVM report estimated total tire-wear emissions to the Dutch environment at about 17,300 tons per year, with about 1,800 tons going to water.
A later RIVM page says about 900 tons of tire-wear microplastics were emitted to the air in the Netherlands in 2012, which it puts at 5 percent of total tire-wear emissions.

The estimates are old and approximate. They suggest that the airborne fraction, the one a wheel-side collector can reach, is a minority of the mass, and that mass is not the same as harm. Whether the 24 and 42 percent refer to that airborne fraction or to a larger one is the question the page leaves open.

The Tyre Collective, a London company that grew out of a master's project at Imperial College London and the Royal College of Art, publishes numbers with explicit denominators in its 2024 impact report. It says its devices capture up to 10 percent of airborne particles by mass on roads and up to 80 percent in the laboratory, that the device captures particles from 0.3 to 217 microns, and that up to 95 percent of the collected mass is non-exhaust emissions and 88 percent tire wear.
Those are one company's figures for a different device with different test conditions, and they cannot be set against VENTRA's simulated shares. They show what a stated denominator looks like.

blocks.x: Why the rules arrived now

r: Euro 7, Regulation (EU) 2024/1257 of April 24, 2024, brings non-exhaust emissions into vehicle type-approval. Its preamble says tires are estimated to be the largest source of microplastics released into the environment and that, as vehicles electrify, non-exhaust emissions are expected to make up up to 90 percent of all particles emitted by road transport by 2050.
The Regulation applies from November 29, 2026 for new types of cars and light vans (categories M1 and N1) and from November 29, 2027 for all new ones.

Its brake particle limits for the standard driving cycle, which apply until the end of 2029, are 3 milligrams per kilometer of PM10 for pure electric vehicles and 7 for the other powertrains in the main M1 and N1 table, with a second stage planned from 2030.
That 3 versus 7 matches what the VENTRA page says about regenerative braking cutting brake wear.

Tire abrasion works differently. The Regulation sets a start date for tire abrasion limits, July 1, 2028 for new C1 tires, and tells the Commission to set limits where the United Nations working party has not agreed uniform provisions by deadlines running from July 1, 2026 (C1 tires) to April 1, 2030 (C3 tires).
The table of limit values in the text I read has no figures in its cells, so I found no tire abrasion number to report.
Some press coverage says Euro 7 sets tire and brake limits from November 2026.
The text says brake limits from then, and tire limits later.
Euro 7 limits what a vehicle sheds. In the text I read it does not address what a capture device collects and who handles it.
That gap is the one this essay is about.

blocks.x: What the captured material is in law

r: European waste law defines waste as any substance or object which the holder discards or intends or is required to discard.

A bag of dust lifted from a collector is therefore a candidate for waste classification in the ordinary course. The directive in its 2008 text gives two routes out. A by-product is something resulting from a production process whose primary aim is not that item, and it needs four conditions, among them certain further use, use without further processing beyond normal industrial practice, and a lawful use that does not lead to overall adverse environmental or human health impacts.

End-of-waste status needs a recovery operation and criteria that include a market or demand, technical requirements for the specific purpose, compliance with product legislation, and no overall adverse impacts. It names tires among the wastes for which end-of-waste criteria should be considered, which says nothing about tire-wear dust in particular, and it lets Member States decide case by case where no EU criteria exist.

This is the 2008 text as published in the Official Journal; the Directive has been amended since, so the current version needs checking. I do not say how any regulator would classify VENTRA's dust. I say the question has a defined legal vocabulary, and a project that wants to show the destination of its material would have to answer in it.

Composition matters to that answer. The Tyre Collective says tire wear is a micronised rubber with 470 organic components, including 6PPD and its derivative 6PPD-quinone, which it describes as acute water toxins, and that particles below 100 microns leach more toxins than larger ones.

Its collected mass is not pure tire either, by its own measurement, so a sample from a car's wheel zone could include road, brake and tire material in proportions that depend on the vehicle and the route.

The US Environmental Protection Agency's own explainer says the tire chemical 6PPD, added to stop tires degrading in ozone, forms 6PPD-quinone when it reacts with ozone, that a 2021 study in Science linked coho salmon deaths to that compound in stormwater, and that limited information is available on its emissions, fate and transport, and human health effects.
That is a reason the composition of any captured fraction is not a detail. VENTRA's pages do not give the composition of what T.R.A.C.E. collects.

blocks.x: Where the dust could go

r: The team's answer, so far, is an enamel coating. Its project page says captured particles can be lifted off the collection surfaces and processed into new material rather than discarded, and that to demonstrate it the team worked captured particulate matter into an enamel coating used inside the car, where the particles are encapsulated.

The design report, which is the only outside source I found that names the enamel, says the material can be removed with water or a vacuum and that some of it now sits in an enamel coating in the cabin.
The word safely appears on the team's page and has no test behind it in anything I read.
The Tyre Collective shows a wider range, all of it stated by the company. Its website lists bitumen, shoe soles and soundproofing as possible uses.

Its 2024 report describes design collaborations shown at Material Matters during London Design Festival in September 2023: pellets made with 20 percent tire particles and recycled PLA for robotic 3D printing, a brooch, and work with a Queen Mary University research group on carbonised tire particles in battery coin cells and pressure sensors.
The same report lists, as a goal for 2026, securing partnerships to scale reuse applications.
So a company that has run 11 pilots with industry partners presents scaled reuse as a goal for 2026, not as a finished route.

The VENTRA team has a precedent for the pattern. Its 2022 car ZEM carried direct air capture filters that, the team says, capture and store carbon dioxide while the car is driven, and its page gives 2 kilograms of CO2 captured per 10,000 kilometers.
That page says the CO2 is stored and does not say what happens to it afterward.
I read this as the same habit one car earlier, a clear account of capture and a short one of destination, and I stress that it is a reading of two pages and not a finding about either team's plans.

blocks.x: The questions for the person with the container

r: A first account would trace one collection. It would say what was collected, over what distance and in what conditions; how much went into the enamel; where the rest went; who received it and under what conditions; and what the receiving party would need before accepting a batch. The maker can say what they hope to supply, and the next organization can say what it is prepared to receive. The two statements need not match yet.

Three identities should stay separate in any caption: the device, the labeled captured fraction and the named next stage. A photograph of the orange wheel caps shows where capture happens. It does not show what was caught.
The team's pages and Dutch Design Week's listing together give a clear picture of the first of the three.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I found no independent test of T.R.A.C.E. The capture shares are the team's simulation figures, and two outlets repeat them as such.
The composition of the collected material, the quantity collected so far, the share used in the enamel, the enamel's composition and any release or durability test are not in the pages I read.
Whether the car's brake particles are captured at a measured rate is not stated.
The student count differs among the team's listing, its overview page and a news report.

I could not open the OECD publication on non-exhaust emissions, because the OECD site returned HTTP 403, so I do not rely on it. I also did not reach the Euro 7 limits for tire abrasion, which the Regulation leaves to later acts.
The RIVM figures are from 2012 and 2016.
The Tyre Collective's numbers are the company's own.
The Waste Framework Directive text is the 2008 version.
The question I would ask the team is the plain one: when the container is full, who is expected to take it, and under what name does the law know what is inside?

posts.title: The press pass gets you through the door. Then what?
posts.subtitle: What Dutch Design Week's accreditation grants and asks, what the Dutch journalism guideline requires once you are inside, and why one 2026 exhibition makes the question concrete.
posts.seoTitle: The press pass gets you through the door. Then what?
posts.description: What Dutch Design Week's press accreditation grants and asks, and what the Dutch Leidraad requires of a reporter once inside.

r: Dutch Design Week asks anyone applying for press accreditation to name up to three subjects they plan to report on, so the first piece of preparation is one the festival requires before it grants access.

That small fact organizes this essay. A pass settles who may enter. It says nothing about who will explain an object, whether a conversation may be recorded, which image may be published, or what an editor will need later. This essay reads the festival's own press pages, the current Leidraad of the Dutch Council for Journalism, which is the profession's self-regulatory guideline, and the program page of one exhibition whose subject is access, and asks what each tells a reporter to prepare. It uses published sources only. It describes no pass of mine, no invitation and no visit, and Dutch Design Week runs October 17 to 25, 2026.

blocks.x: What the festival gives you, and what it asks

r: The press page frames the 2026 edition under the theme R.A.W., Rebel Authentic Worth, and says Dutch Design Week presents the work of 2,500 designers to 350,000 visitors at around one hundred locations across the city. It lists five resources: accreditation, press releases, brand assets, press clippings and an image library.

The accreditation page says press accreditation grants access to all locations, talks, conferences, press tours on request and select networking events, and that press tours are available only during the first weekend.

The form asks for a media profession from a list that includes freelance editor or journalist, media creator and press photographer. It asks for recent coverage of Dutch Design Week or proof of publication of a similar event signed with the applicant's name, with up to five links. It asks for one to three subjects, for any interviews the applicant plans to request with specific designers, studios or locations, and whether the applicant wants to join a press tour.

The page is not fully consistent. It says accreditation for ddw26 is open and then refers to Dutch Design Week 2025 and to October 18 to 26, 2025. It describes the first-weekend tour as October 18 and 19, while the form offers October 17 and 18 as choices.
The press page and the September 29, 2026 press release give the festival dates as October 17 to 25.
I read the accreditation text as partly carried over from the previous edition. A reporter planning tours should confirm dates with the press office directly.

blocks.x: Four resources, four kinds of evidence

r: The resources do different jobs. Accreditation is access. A press release is an attributed account by the organizer. The September 29, 2026 release, for instance, says more than 2,500 designers take part in the 26th edition, names the new hubs for collectible and digital design, and lists highlight projects with a credited image for each, such as the TU/ecomotive VENTRA image credited to its team.
The image library holds photographs for which the festival asks users to always credit Dutch Design Week and the photographer, and its entries list a date, an area and a photographer.
When I read it, the newest entries listed were from October 18, 2025.
The press clippings page lets a reader filter coverage by year from 2023 to 2026, by country and by type, newspaper or website.
Brand assets are logos and banners.

Keeping those apart is the discipline. A release's claim is the organizer's claim. An image library photograph supports a caption and a credit and does not support a claim about what an object does. A clipping is someone else's reporting, to be read and checked and not taken as a source of fact. The accreditation form, for its part, records what the reporter said they would cover, which is a record worth keeping beside the final piece.

blocks.x: A case where the subject is access

r: Table of Power is an exhibition at de Kruisruimte on Generaal Bothastraat in Eindhoven, hosted by SHOW NOT SHOW, with a Dutch Design Week ticket required.

Its program page says a long table stands at the heart of the exhibition and provides the setting for the official Dutch Design Week opening dinner for the international press, a gathering it describes as bringing together people who influence what the design world sees, discusses and remembers.

The title refers to Jacqueline Hassink's project The Table of Power, in which she photographed boardroom tables of major multinationals, and the page says SHOW NOT SHOW turns the table from a symbol of institutional power into a platform for participation and interpretation.

Hassink's project has its own record on access. The Rencontres d'Arles artist page says her first art project photographed the boardroom tables of Europe's forty largest multinational corporations, without people in the frame, and that the collaborating companies filled out a questionnaire about the tables.

A bookseller's listing quotes the photobook historians Martin Parr and Gerry Badger as saying that of the forty companies approached, only 21 allowed a photograph, and that those that refused appear in the book as black photographs.
I rely on that quotation for the count and have not seen the book.

For a reporter the exhibition poses a plain question about a double role. A journalist invited to a dinner that the organizer hosts for the press is a guest and a witness at once. The Leidraad asks journalists to work independently and to avoid conflicts of interest and the appearance of them, and to be transparent about their assignment and approach where relevant.

That is a general rule and not a comment on any invitation. The program page does not say who attends the dinner, how press are invited, or what recording terms apply; it says only what the table is for.
Those are separate questions, and the honest plan keeps them separate from the premise.

blocks.x: What the Leidraad asks of a reporter inside

r: The Leidraad in force since September 2026 is a Dutch-language document, and I paraphrase it in English. It describes itself as the basis for the Council's decisions on whether journalism was careful, and invites anyone who does journalism, on any platform, to use it as a starting point.

On preparation and conduct it says journalists make themselves known as journalists to potential interviewees and are clear about their journalistic intentions, also when entering spaces that are not public. When they interview someone, they should tell the person enough about the nature of the publication that the person can decide whether to take part. It allows a journalist to record a telephone call without telling the other party, and requires telling them before publication if a recorded call is to be used in whole or in part. It states that sources are in principle named in publications.
An embargo that a journalist accepts must be kept until the agreed term ends, and it lapses if the information is published elsewhere or the requester lifts it or breaks the agreement.

Three of its norms bear directly on a visit that feeds several pieces. Quotes from interviews may not be used in a different context from the one the interviewee could expect from what the journalist told them, and if the nature or content of the publication changes during editing so that it no longer matches that expectation, the person must be asked for permission again.
Footage may not be used to illustrate another subject, or with a context other than that for which it was made, unless it is made clear why it was used.
Photographs and footage of people in spaces that are not generally accessible may not be published without their consent, with a narrow exception for evident wrongdoing.
The Leidraad also asks writers to separate facts, claims and opinions.

blocks.x: Images, quotes and names under Dutch copyright law

r: Dutch copyright law adds its own layer for the images and quotes a reporter brings home. In the unofficial English translation by Mireille van Eechoud, which reflects the Act as in force on January 1, 2012 and needs checking against the current text, Article 15a allows quotation from a lawfully published work in an announcement, review, polemic or scientific treatise or a piece with a comparable purpose, if the quoting accords with social custom, the quoted parts are justified by the purpose, the maker's right to be named is observed and the source and the maker's name are clearly indicated where reasonably possible.
Article 25(1)(a) gives the maker a right to oppose publication of the work without a mention of their name, unless opposing would be unreasonable.
This is a statute, not a press-room rule, and I use it only to show why the credit line travels with the image: the festival's own rule to credit the photographer matches the legal logic.

blocks.x: Consent means different things under different legal footing

r: The Dutch Data Protection Authority's English guidance on publishing personal data online says that under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) you need consent from the people concerned in most cases, and that people who gave consent can later withdraw or change it.

It also describes a journalistic exception: it applies to an activity whose sole purpose is to communicate information, opinions or ideas to the public, whatever the medium, it requires weighing interests such as the contribution to a debate of public interest and how well known the person is, and it still needs a legal basis.
Where the exception applies, the guidance says the author does not have to ask consent, and consent once given, for example to publish an interview, cannot be withdrawn.

That matters for a record. A person's consent to be photographed or quoted can have a different legal weight depending on whether the publication is journalism in that sense or something else, and the word "sole" in the authority's description is a reason to keep the purposes of each format clear. I draw no conclusion about any particular piece. I point to the authority's page because it shows that "they said yes" is a fact to write down with its date and scope, not a permanent permission.

blocks.x: One visit, several pieces, one record

r: The Leidraad's context rule suggests what a capture record should hold for each conversation or image. It should say what the person was told about the publication, which formats they agreed to, whether they may be named, who owns any image they supplied, and what was promised about review.

A friendly conversation is not a blanket release, and a record that preserves each answer lets one visit feed an article, a short video and a social post without asking the same question twice or stretching a quote past the context in which it was given.

The Dutch Design Week materials suggest the other half: for each item, note its type (organizer's account, image-library photograph, own capture, third-party coverage) so the final piece cites each for what it can support.

At the desk the first decision for each item is plain: edit next, needs a source, needs permission, or park. That four-way list is a proposed practice and not a standard, and I do not claim it has been tested in the field.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I have no knowledge of any press pass, invitation or assignment, and nothing here says one exists or does not. The accreditation page is partly out of date, so its tour dates and the scope of access need confirmation.
The Table of Power page does not state who can attend the dinner or under what terms.
The Leidraad is the profession's self-regulatory guideline and not law, and I paraphrase it from Dutch.
The Parr and Badger count rests on a bookseller's quotation.
The Dutch Copyright Act translation reflects 2012.
I did not read the exhibition's press kit, which the program page links on a file-sharing site.
The question I would take to any opening is the practical one: for each thing I bring home, who said I could use it, in what form, and where is that written down?

posts.title: What is the sensor actually telling you?
posts.subtitle: KojiGotchi turns sensor readings into a face. Its open firmware, its published experiments and the parts' own datasheets show what that face can and cannot say.
posts.seoTitle: What is the sensor actually telling you?
posts.description: KojiGotchi turns sensor readings into a face. Its open firmware, experiments and datasheets show what that face can and cannot say.

r: In the published firmware for the KojiGotchi prototype, the avatar's most cheerful face appears only when six separate checks pass at once, and its saddest only when every group of checks fails at once.

That is a design decision, and the project made it visible by publishing its code. This essay follows one reading from sensor to face using the project's own pages, its open repository and the datasheets of two of its parts. It uses published sources only. It reports no device test, no visit and no interview, and Dutch Design Week itself runs October 17 to 25, 2026.

blocks.x: What the project is

r: The Dutch Design Week 2026 program lists KojiGotchi: A Tamagotchi for the Microbial Age as a free exhibition at BioArt Laboratories on Strijp T+R. It describes an open-source wearable that uses human body heat to grow Aspergillus oryzae, the fungus behind miso and sake, with a digital avatar called KojiMoji that reads live sensor data and translates environmental conditions into emotional states.

The listing says the project began with experiments at DTU Biosustain in Copenhagen for the 2025 Biodesign Challenge, led by Maxim Velli with electronics by Rasmus Emil Tofthøj, visual identity by Tania Safa and narrative by Taylor Rayne, with Mark Torochkin redesigning the casing for Dutch Design Week, and supervision by Dr. Adrien Rigobello and Dr. Joshua Evans.

The listing and the project site state the purpose as cultural rather than technical: the argument is that biodesign pictures futures of living with microbes while most people have not built the sensibility to do so, and that a Tamagotchi-style companion could help.
The site says the device is designed for primary schools, maker spaces and home kitchens, and that the team is collecting interest to decide whether to produce a first batch.
I treat it as a speculative design and education project with working electronics, which is how its own pages present it.

blocks.x: The parts, and a version problem

r: The repository README lists two prototypes. The Full one runs on an ESP32 board with an ENS160 plus AHT22 air-quality module, a DS18B20 temperature probe, an HD-38 moisture sensor, an SD card module, an OLED screen and three buttons. The Mini one runs on a smaller ESP32 board with only an AHT21 air temperature and humidity sensor, the screen and three buttons.
The Experiments page names the same components and adds a TCS34725 color sensor that was tested and dropped.

So the answer to what the sensor is telling you depends on the version. A Mini cannot report a volatile-organic-compound reading, a probe temperature or a moisture value, because it has none of those sensors.
The website's KojiMoji demo, by contrast, shows four inputs: temperature, humidity, volatile organic compounds labeled as smell, and carbon dioxide.
The listing does not say which prototype or what firmware version will be on show.
The part name itself varies: AHT22 on the website and in the README, AHT21 in the labels of the code.
I could not tell from these pages whether that is one chip or two.

blocks.x: Reading one number

r: Take the carbon dioxide input. The website lists the ENS160 as the sensor for carbon dioxide and volatile organic compounds, and the code reads two values from it, an eCO2 and a TVOC.
The ENS160 datasheet says the chip is a metal-oxide gas sensor whose on-chip algorithms calculate CO2-equivalents, TVOC and air-quality indices.

It explains that its eCO2 output reverses a historical correlation between volatile organic compounds and the CO2 that people exhale, providing "ppm CO2-equivalents" from measured VOCs plus hydrogen, with a stated output range of 400 to 65,000.
In other words, the number is an index of volatile compounds expressed on a carbon dioxide scale, and the correlation behind it comes from air in rooms where people breathe.

The datasheet does not say what that index means beside a bowl of fermenting rice, and I make no claim that it is wrong there. I note that the website's demo opens with carbon dioxide at 400 ppm, which is the bottom of the output range the datasheet specifies.

The datasheet also says its accuracy figures come from tests in clean, partially synthetic air in a climate chamber at 25 degrees Celsius and 50 percent humidity, which may not reflect real-life environments, and that after a first power-on the chip needs an hour before its outputs are usable and about three minutes after each later start. It adds that the change in sensor resistance is greatest in the first 48 hours of operation.
The team's sensor tests ran 72 hours.
Temperature is on firmer ground. The DS18B20 probe's datasheet gives an accuracy of plus or minus 0.5 degrees Celsius from minus 10 to plus 85.
The team says the probe detected a difference of 1 degree between the air and the rice interior, which it uses to argue that users can be prompted to mix the koji.
That difference is twice the stated accuracy of a single sensor, and the pages do not say how the two readings were compared.

blocks.x: What was done to the numbers

r: The experiments page is unusually direct about processing. Of four experiments labeled first_try to fourth_try, it says two failed, and the two graphs shown come from third_try (temperature) and fourth_try (color). The temperature readings were factored so the flat section at the start corresponds to 30 degrees, and the rest were adjusted accordingly.
The temperature graph shows an average and standard deviation for three runs, and the color graph the same for two.
The raw data and the notebooks used to plot them are linked from the page.
Two naming details are worth noticing. The page numbers its experiments 1 to 4, and the graph notes use another sequence, first_try to fourth_try, so "fourth_try" does not mean Experiment 4.

And the project's product page and its experiments page tell the first experiments slightly differently. The product page says the pocket-bag test showed a small amount of growth. The experiments page says it yielded minimal to no visible growth.

The product page also describes a roughly 60-hour proof of concept with koji in the lower compartment of a 3D-printed egg-shaped container, while the experiments page has the egg container carrying only a sensor for 48 hours and puts the 60-hour koji proof in the later transparent chamber.
These accounts could both be right if there were extra runs, and I could not resolve them from the pages.

blocks.x: The rule: when the face changes

r: The rule is in the code. The firmware published on GitHub, linked from the project's resources page, was created on June 10, 2025 and last pushed on June 24, 2025, under an MIT license.

In it, the optimal range for koji is 25 to 35 degrees Celsius for temperature and 70 to 90 percent for air humidity. The moisture sensor's raw reading, where 0 is wet and 4095 is dry, counts as good between 1000 and 2500, as too wet below 800 and too dry above 3000.
The carbon dioxide thresholds are 1000 and 2000 ppm and the volatile organic compound thresholds are 50, 200 and 500 ppb, and the code marks both sets with the comment "Example."

The base face is chosen in three branches. The very happy face is drawn when the air temperature, the air humidity, the probe temperature and the moisture all fall in range and the eCO2 is under 1000 and the TVOC under 200. The very sad face is drawn only when the air temperature, humidity and probe temperature are all out of range, the moisture is too wet or too dry, and either gas value is at or above its first threshold. Every other combination gets the sad face.
Separate overlays then add icons for cold or warm, humidity high or low, rice good, wet or dry, and carbon dioxide and volatile-compound levels.

Three consequences follow from the code as written, and I state them as readings of the code. A single out-of-range value produces the sad face, so the face does not distinguish a small deviation from a large one. Moisture readings between 800 and 1000 or between 2500 and 3000 are neither good nor wet nor dry, so they prevent the happiest face and trigger no moisture icon.
And a middle happy face is defined in the file, and I found no place where it is drawn.
I did not find a test for a missing or failed reading from the probe, and the code reports initialization failures only for the screen, the AHT sensor and the ENS160.
None of this is a defect claim. The thresholds are commented as examples, and the project calls itself a work in progress.

blocks.x: From face to action

r: The device is meant to teach. The guidebook, according to the project's resources page, teaches principles of cleanliness and optimal conditions through do's and don'ts, and encourages users to rely on their nose and observation.
The product page says koji's aroma gives immediate sensory feedback on the success of caretaking.
The face is one cue among three, with smell and sight.

The project's own user study shows why the other cues matter. In an interactive session, participants set up the device themselves with rice flour as a prop for spores, and the team reports that not a single participant considered or attempted to work in a sterile manner. Participants generally preferred white koji and found black and green varieties too dangerous in appearance.

The online survey reported that 84.78 percent were curious about or fully comfortable with contributing body heat to microbial growth, while 39.13 percent said they would trust food fermented by such a device.
Those percentages are consistent with 46 respondents, which would be 39 and 18 people. The page does not state the number, so that is my arithmetic and not their count.

The team's treatment of contamination is where sensing stops. The experiments page says mold color is a key visual cue for potential contamination and that overheating inside the rice clump made koji prone to it, which is why the probe and a color sensor were added.

The color sensor produced a confusing mid-experiment peak while the koji visibly greened, and changing room light made a portable version harder, so the team chose a transparent growth chamber so the wearer can see the koji.
The sensor that was supposed to read contamination was replaced by the person's eyes. Nothing in the parts list measures contamination directly.

Food safety is a subject for specialists, and the project does not claim a medical or regulatory finding. For context, a 2025 industrial review of Aspergillus oryzae notes that the species is closely related to the pathogenic A. flavus, that wild strains have the potential to make three mycotoxins, that aflatoxin has not been found in A. oryzae in the strict sense, and that mycotoxin production in some strains is thought to be induced by adverse growth conditions.

That review concerns industrial strains, not the spores a hobbyist buys, and I draw no conclusion about the device. I mention it so that a reader understands why the cleanliness advice in the guidebook is not decoration.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I did not see a KojiGotchi device, and the listing does not say which version will be on show.
I do not know how the avatar's thresholds were chosen; the code calls two of them examples, and the experiments page reports the 25 to 35 degree range and no humidity range.
I did not review the raw data files.
The firmware I read was last pushed in June 2025, and the 2026 build, with a redesigned casing, may differ.
The datasheet comparisons use two parts whose exact variants on the device I could not confirm.
The product and experiments pages differ on early experiments.
The question I would ask the team at the exhibit is the one the avatar invites. If the face turns sad, what is the wearer supposed to do first, and who wrote that instruction?
